speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: RIMOUSKI, QUEBEC  RED RIVER VALLEY, MANITOBA  FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this last week end has been one of great anxiety, even suffering and distress, for a large number of our fellow citizens, especially in two separate areas of this country. When I heard yesterday of the terrible fire that was raging at Rimou-ski I sent telegrams to the mayor and to the archbishop, which perhaps I might read, because I feel sure that all hon. members would like to be associated with the sentiments I expressed in these telegrams.
The telegram to the mayor was as follows:
A Son Honneur le Maire Victor Lepage Rimouski, Que.
Je suis horrific d'apprendre l'etendue du sinistre que vient de subir la ville de Rimouski. A la population de votre ville et en particulier aux families, aux institutions et aux rr.aisons d'affaires si durement eprouvees, vous voudrez bien trans-mettre l'assurance de ma plus entiere sympathie.
Louis-S. St-Laurent
The telegram to the archbishop reads as follows:
A Son Excellence Mgr Courchesne, ArchevSque de Rimouski,
Rimouski. Que.
La nouvelle de la tragique conflagration de Rimouski me cause un vif chagrin. Je tiens a vous adresser, a vous, ainsi qu'aux autorites du semi-naire et des autres institutions religieuses qui ont etd eprouvees, 1'assurance de ma tres vive sympathie.	*
Louis-S. St-Laurent
In this morning's Montreal Gazette the message to Mayor Lepage is translated as follows:
I am horrified to learn the extent of the disaster Rimouski has suffered. To the population of your city, and especially to the families, the institutions and the business firms so badly affected, I would ask you to convey the assurance of my deepest sympathy.
The message to Archbishop Courchesne is translated as follows:
The news of the tragic conflagration at Rimouski causes me deep sorrow. I would wish to extend to you and to the authorities of the seminary and of the other religious institutions which have suffered losses the assurance of my deepest sympathy.
Some hours earlier we learned that flood conditions in the Red river valley had taken a turn for the worse. Last Saturday I gave the following statement to the press:
From end to end of Canada, the people are deeply concerned about the anxiety of their fellow citizens in Winnipeg and the Red river valley. We are all anxious to have done whatever can be done to relieve the distress and suffering of those whose homes have been invaded by the floods. All agencies of all governments, as well as the Red Cross and other voluntary organizations, are doing all they can to help, and we all hope that the disastrous conditions may soon be ended.
Over the week end the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) went to Winnipeg to see that everything that could be done Ijy agencies of the federal government was being done. He returned this morning and brought the following letter to me from the premier of Manitoba:
May 7, 1950
Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent, P.C., K.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
As you will know by reports that have already reached you, our flood situation, which we had hoped would by now have passed its peak, is becoming increasingly serious. Recent heavy rains throughout most of the Red river valley area have added tremendously to the volume of water, the area of flooding and resulting damage. For two or

Fire and Flood Damage three days during the worst of the rain and following it, extremely high winds caused still further damage, making relief activities very difficult and in some cases impossible. From the international boundary north to lake Winnipeg, an area some seventy miles long and varying in width from five to thirty miles is now covered with flood waters. This area includes many towns and villages, greater Winnipeg and the city of St. Boniface. In greater Winnipeg itself, in spite of emergency diking operations, several areas containing not only a large number of residences but three large hospitals and other public buildings, already have been in large part evacuated.
The situation took such a sudden turn for the worse late last Friday afternoon as to indicate the necessity of immediate action to evacuate two hospitals and two large residential areas; I therefore convened late that night an emergent meeting of representatives of some of the organizations most active in flood relief, including representatives of the army, the Manitoba Red Cross Society and of the police, engineering and health departments of the city of Winnipeg.
Hon. Stuart Garson, Minister of Justice, had just come to the city for the purpose of investigating the flood situation and conferring with our government regarding it, so we were fortunate in being able to have him sit in at this emergency conference.
Following a full discussion at this meeting, it was unanimously agreed that the situation had become so serious that all flood relief efforts should be centralized immediately. Acting on this advice, with the meeting still in progress, and with the approval of everyone present, I asked the army to take charge of the co-ordinating operation, it being understood that all other organizations and individuals would continue to give their full co-operation and assistance. Your colleague, the Minister of Defence, was good enough to approve of the army under Brigadier R. E. A. Morton acting in this capacity.
As you are aware, the province of Manitoba already has been receiving all the federal aid which we have asked for and that is a great deal. Practically a month ago army headquarters here and I had discussed the possibility of a flood this spring and had made full arrangements regarding the circumstances in which the army would be called upon to assist. The actual document covering this agreement was signed by me on April 13 last. Similarly, the navy and the air force, though not operating under a specific agreement, have extended to the province and to all other agencies at work on flood relief, the utmost co-operation.	The
R.C.M.P., in which of course both the federal and provincial governments are interested, has also given us service and co-operation, leaving nothing to be desired. It is unnecessary for me to mention other federal assistance, such as district engineers, department officials, and by no means least of all, your own two ministers, Mr. Claxton and Mr. Garson, having done everything possible to help in this emergency. I would like, therefore, to express to you our deep appreciation of the wholehearted assistance that has been so readily forthcoming from all federal agencies. Exactly the same is true, I am glad to say, of the municipalities, local and volunteer organizations throughout the area and the province.
In spite of all this effort, however, the situation became not only serious but critical last Friday, resulting, as mentioned, in my declaring a state of emergency, and asking the army to assume overall charge of all flood relief activity. It is still critical, and I feel that its effects are so great as to require in many cases expenditures so large that they are beyond the capacity of individuals, organizations, municipalities and even the provincial government, to assume.

Under these circumstances, and again assuring you that this province greatly appreciates the assistance already given, I would request that you formally recognize this situation as a national emergency and let us have your assurance of federal financial assistance commensurate with our needs. I am unable at present to state what these will ultimately be. All the people best qualified to prepare an estimate have been, and still are, too busy with the emergency of the flood for me to ask them to given even a casual estimate. In fairness to them, I feel that they should not attempt a considered estimate until the floods have subsided. Several of my cabinet colleagues, departmental officials and others have, however, along with me, conferred with Hon. Stuart Garson during his much appreciated three days here. We feel that he has a good understanding of our position in this matter. What I would request at the present time is that you give us the assurance that assistance will be forthcoming from the federal government. My officials and I will be glad to meet with your government's representatives in order to discuss details of the arrangement.
I wish to thank you in advance for the consideration that I know you will give to this request from the province of Manitoba which has had the misfortune to suffer such a catastrophe at this 1950 flood.
Yours sincerely,
Douglas Campbell
On receipt of this communication from the premier of Manitoba I immediately called a special meeting of council. Following the meeting I dispatched to the premier of Manitoba by telegram the following reply:
Ottawa, May, 8, 1950
Hon. D. L. Campbell, M.L.A.,
Premier of Manitoba,
Winnipeg, Man.
Immediately upon his return to Ottawa, Hon. Stuart Garson delivered to me your letter of May 7, 1950, outlining the present position with regard to the serious floods in the Red river valley in your province. We are glad that all of the federal agencies and authorities in your province have been extending to you any assistance which you required since this is what they had been instructed to do.
We have been following the development of this flood closely from the beginning. We felt that the heavy snowfall in the Red river valley, especially in the American part of it, coupled with the late spring break-up, was bound to create some measure of flooding on the Canadian side. The transformation of this serious condition into one of really critical proportions by the untimely and heavy rains and winds of the past few days is a misfortune of the first order.
In view of the serious news which comes out of the United States part of the Red river valley to the effect that heavy rains there may possibly create another flood crest, we entirely agree with you that the immediate efforts of your government and our own in this matter should be directed towards meeting this physical threat of flooding. But we can assure you that as soon as you feel free to open up the question of federal financial assistance, upon the basis of this being beyond your capacity to deal with alone, we shall be glad indeed to discuss it with you.
No doubt you will want to know now in general terms upon what basis financial assistance to you will be considered. Until the extent of your misfortune is determined, no one can be specific, but I

can say in general terms that in arriving at the amount of our assistance to you, we shall apply the same principles as those upon which our assistance to the British Columbia government in connection with the Fraser river valley floods was determined.
Louis S. St. Laurent
In the case of the disastrous fire at Rimouski, the federal government has taken precisely the same kind of immediate action that was taken at the very beginning of the flood in the Red river valley and that has been taken in respect to other disasters. The special facilities of the armed forces and all other federal agencies in the area were made available at once to assist in emergency action and the provision of emergency relief.
I merely want to repeat that I am sure all the people of Canada sympathize with those who have had the misfortune to be overtaken by these catastrophic events.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: RIMOUSKI, QUEBEC  RED RIVER VALLEY, MANITOBA  FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of this house will join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in the expression of sympathy he has conveyed to the citizens of Rimouski in the appalling disaster that struck that community during the past week end. We all regard that expression of sympathy as voiced not only on behalf of the members of this house, but on behalf of the people of Canada, following one of the worst and most tragic disasters that have occurred in this country.
Hon. members also will be pleased to learn of the steps that have been taken with respect to the situation in Manitoba, though I believe there is room for further comment on another occasion as to the way in which certain things might have been done, which this tragic event will emphasize.
These disasters bring vividly and dramatically to our attention the fact that any community in this country, large or small, may be visited some time by a calamity far beyond the power of municipal facilities to cope with, and far beyond the ability of the citizens of that community to deal with effectively. Rimouski is already looking to the future and seeing what may be done to repair the damage that has been done; it has been estimated locally that it will require at least a quarter of a century to do it.
There is still great emergency in Manitoba. These events, entirely different in character, nevertheless demonstrate the need in every community of some voluntary civilian organization to deal with emergencies of this kind.
For some years since the end of the war the need for civilian defence forces has been under consideration. These tragedies might well suggest to us that we should not limit
Fire and Flood Damage our thinking in that connection to situations of a military or semi-military character, but should recognize that without warning a disaster as great as that resulting from war itself may call for the immediate well-organized efforts of the citizens of that community, of the surrounding countryside, or even of the whole country. So it would seem that these two events, having regard to their magnitude and the agony which has accompanied them, should impress upon all of us the desirability of creating the kind of organization that has been so clearly and ably suggested from time to time by General Worthington-not merely in order to deal with the direct or indirect effects of war but in order to deal with any emergency that may arise.
Both in Rimouski and in Winnipeg there are stories .of the magnificent heroism of people who have risked everything, not only to save their own families and their own homes, but to help others; and in so doing they have been actuated by the most unselfish motives and worked to the point of utter exhaustion. But no matter how wholehearted and unselfish may have been their effort, the inescapable fact remains that no integrated municipal or community organization existed for this purpose.
As we extend our sympathy and the offer of the support and assistance of the people of Canada on this occasion, I would strongly urge hon. members to think of the lesson these tragedies have brought home, and consider the advisability of the early organization of voluntary civilian forces to deal with any such occurrence in the future.

maintopic: RIMOUSKI, QUEBEC  RED RIVER VALLEY, MANITOBA  FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we wish to join with all hon. members in expressing our sympathy to those who have suffered in these great disasters of the past few days. The sudden and overwhelming fire in Rimouski, bringing loss and tragedy, I think has pointed up the innumerable smaller catastrophies affecting many others in this country which we have suffered from time to time, particularly in recent months. This is one phase of the disaster at Rimouski that should cause us to think of fire protection and precautions against fire all across Canada, in order that property and human life may be saved.
I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will take the same steps with respect to Rimouski that he proposes to take in regard to the flood in the Red river valley. Those of us who know what was done in the Fraser valley in British Columbia under similar circumstances are glad to know that the government contemplates the same pattern of relief for the Red river valley. I hope that

Fire and Flood Damage similar and generous assistance may also be extended to the citizens of Rimouski.
In mentioning Rimouski, may I say how much I regret that the member for Rimouski (Mr. Belzile) is lying gravely ill in a hospital in this city. His personal loss in the destruction of his home, and the fact that he is unable to speak to his constituency at this time, are circumstances which we deeply regret.
So far as the flood in Manitoba is concerned, I hope that steps will be taken immediately by the governments of Canada and the United States to ensure that disasters like those which have occurred in the Red river valley within the last century and a half will be prevented in the days to come.
We wish to express our sympathy to the people of the Red river valley, and to those who have suffered devastation and loss as a result of the Are in Rimouski.

Mr. Speaker, as representative of a lower St. Lawrence constituency almost adjoining that of Rimouski, I heartily echo the. feelings of sympathy which the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. party have expressed for the people of Rimouski.
I was passing through Quebec yesterday when I heard of the catastrophe. I immediately got in touch with localities in the vicinity of Rimouski in order to find out about the situation and to make sure that the good people of the stricken city received the assistance they required.
I also contacted federal authorities, especially the Prime Minister's secretary in Ottawa. It was reassuring to learn that the Prime Minister himself was already giving personal attention to the Rimouski disaster.
This tragedy affects me all the more since for more than five years I had the honour of attending the seminary of Rimouski which was partially destroyed by the fire.
In addition I was pleased to see the dispatch with which, considering the lack of communications, the military authorities answered the appeal for help that had come from Rimouski, in order to provide every possible assistance, under the circumstances, to these people in distress. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) also placed the services of his department at the disposal of local authorities. The Montreal and Quebec divisions of the Red Cross dispatched relief groups with amazing rapidity.

I should like also to congratulate the civil and religious authorities of Rimouski for organizing relief squads and providing valuable assistance and help to the stricken people.
Early yesterday, both on my own behalf and in the name of my constituents, I offered my sympathy to His Excellency Monsignor Courchesne, archbishop of Rimouski, to the civic authorities-the mayor and aldermen of the city-and I also offered to place myself at their disposal and to substitute for, if possible, their doughty representative (Mr. Belzile) who, as was pointed out a few moments ago by the leader of the C.C.F. party, is confined to the hospital by a serious illness.
I repeat the offer of service I made to my fellow citizens from Rimouski and assure them of my entire devotion in this respect.
And now, to His Excellency Monsignor Courchesne, to the mayor and aldermen of the city of Rimouski, to the authorities of my alma mater, to the clergy and the people of this prosperous lower St. Lawrence city, I once again express my most sincere sympathy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move,

Barter Trading
seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, a report of the Canadian Press dated May 5, 1950, which attributes to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) who sailed this morning to attend the commonwealth economic conference in Sydney, Australia, as the representative of Canada, a statement that he believes an organization will be set up in accordance with his recommendations to this house on March 13, 1950, that an organization be established to promote barter trading between Canada and other nations, which statement of policy is directly contrary to the statement of policy made on behalf of the government on different occasions by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and therefore suggests that at Sydney a plan will be put forward which violates the well-established constitutional principle of collective ministerial responsibility to the House of Commons.

Standing order 31 reads as follows:
(1)	Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business (standing order No. 15) has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
It would therefore appear that the motion as presented at the present time complies with that provision. The second part of the order reads:
(2)	The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter.
The hon. member has done that. The third part of the standing order reads as follows:
(3)	He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.

Standing order 31(6) (c) reads:

My recollection of previous debates in the house during the session is to the effect that this matter was fully discussed at that time. My recollection is that the Minister of Fisheries referred to this matter when he spoke in the house either on the debate in reply to the speech from the throne or on the budget, I am not sure which, and that other hon. members also spoke on the matter at that time. Therefore it occurs to me that it is reviving discussion on a matter that has already been discussed during the present session. Moreover, there is also citation 176, in Beauchesne's third edition, which reads as follows:
The "definite matter of urgent public importance", for the discussion of which the adjournment of the house may be moved under standing order 31, must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
There will be other opportunities to discuss this matter before the organization can be set up. In my opinion, a motion to adjourn the house under this standing order should be very carefully considered before it is put to the house. The business of the house is arranged from day to day, and that business is announced at the close of business of the previous day. A motion under this rule disrupts the arrangements previously made. Hon. members who have come prepared to discuss one matter are suddenly called upon to discuss some other matter. speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. Macnaughion (Mount Royal) moved
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 152, to amend the Canadian Red Cross Society Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this motion for second reading is carried, as I am sure it will be, I think we should note that it is a most interesting coincidence that we should be dealing with a bill respecting the Canadian Red Cross Society on this day. As has already been made clear by the remarks made commencing at three o'clock, the Canadian Red Cross Society has been living up to its great traditions during the past few weeks, and particularly during this past week end in connection with the tragic disasters at Rimouski and at Winnipeg and throughout the Red river valley. It seems to me that everything that was said in this house the last time this bill was up has been more than vindicated. Your Honour will remember that on that occasion members on all sides of the house paid glowing tributes to the work of this organization.
In these two tragic occurrences we have had evidence of what the Red Cross can do and of the speed with which it starts to work wherever there is need. I am sure members of this house will be most anxious to see this bill put through. If I might suggest it to Your Honour, I think this bill will so readily meet with the concurrence of hon. members that this is one instance in which it is hardly necessary for you to suggest that the bill be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills. I am sure that if the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton), who is sponsoring the bill, asks that we go directly into committee of the whole after it has received second reading, no one will object. Among other reasons I think it would be a good idea to get the bill through today so that we can make up for what happened last session. Hon. members will recall that we passed a similar bill last session, thinking we had done a good job, only to discover that our friends in the other place had emasculated the measure in such a way that by the time it got back to us it was not worth putting through. I should like to ask the hon. member for Mount Royal, when we get into committee, wherein the bill,

as it has now been passed in the other place, differs from the bill they rejected last year. I think only a minor detail has been changed. At any rate I hope that the bill can be put through all its stages today, and we shall know this time that after it is passed by this house it will shortly become law.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the bill. As member for a constituency which is pretty much under water at the present time, I want to take the opportunity of saying "many thanks" to the Red Cross. They have come to the rescue again. It is brought forcefully to the attention of people in the danger zone that the Red Cross is doing a wonderful job. On behalf of the people of my constituency I thank the Red Cross for what it has already done in the evacuation of flood victims.
Mr. Speaker-
Order. I should remind the house that if the hon. member speaks now he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, before the debate is concluded I want to make a few brief remarks by way of endorsation of what has been said by previous speakers about the Red Cross. I have a personal reason for being grateful to the Red Cross for their work in Canada. On various occasions I have seen their work in my own community. First of all I want to express my appreciation to the officers of the Canadian Red Cross for providing hon. members with an excellent brief on the history, constitution, policy and program of the Canadian Red Cross Society, prepared by them for members of the Senate and House of Commons. I have read the brief, and I find it quite informative. It is my intention to pass on to others some of the information contained therein, because I know that they will be just as much interested in it as members of the house.
My first direct experience with the Canadian Red Cross was in France during the first world war, and my second was in the Halifax disaster of 1917. Living in a pioneer community, I have noticed throughout the years the excellent work the Red Cross has performed in the isolated districts of my constituency. In 1948 there were serious floods on the Columbia river, and at that time the local organization of the Canadian Red Cross Society did an excellent and valiant job. Only today I picked up a local paper from my constituency and was pleased to find that the Red Cross is still ready to meet
Canadian Red Cross Society Act any emergency. In the Trail Daily Times of May 3, 1950, there is an article under the heading:	"Flood committee prepares for
action." The article reads:
Following on the heels of a request for flood precautionary measures ... a meeting of the disaster committee of the Red Cross Society was held . last night at the city hall. Leo Levey, chairman of the committee, stressed the obligation of the Red Cross that the preparation for disaster must not await the occurrence of a catastrophe but must be planned in advance. The Red Cross committee discussed plans for rescue, transportation, communications, food, shelter, clothing and medical care, and discussed methods of co-ordinating the work with that of other groups in the event of a disaster.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that the people concerned in this organization are prepared to meet any emergent situation. Again I concur in all the remarks made by previous speakers about this most excellent organization.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks about this bill. I want to say at the outset that I am in favour of it. It is my opinion, and the opinion of many others, that the Red Cross has proven to be one of the greatest assets for good that we have in the whole Dominion of Canada. In my own riding it has worked wonders amongst the poorer people, those who have had problems of illness and other adversities with which to contend. The Red Cross has always come to their assistance in every way possible.
In the sparsely settled northern part of my riding there is a Red Cross organization which I do not think can be bettered or equalled by those in other parts of Canada. It is an organization of real people. The good they have done in the last fifteen or twenty years, and the service they have performed in gathering things together to send overseas, has been remarkable. About twenty years ago, a small Red Cross organization started in the village of Wilberforce, with one nurse; now we have a hospital almost in the centre of the county, with six nurses, and it has become inadequate to take care of the situation. We are working on a project for a hospital to take care of the whole county, one which will be more or less a county hospital under the auspices of the Red Cross.
I am wholeheartedly in support of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with hon. members who have already spoken in support of this measure, and of the suggestion that we endeavour to put it through the house this afternoon. There are two branches of the Red Cross with which I have come into contact from time to time. First there is the

Canadian Red Cross Society Act work of the Red Cross in many of the outposts. I have seen what they are doing particularly in the far northern part of Ontario, and I have come to realize of what great benefit the organization is to the people living there. I have also seen the work of the junior Red Cross in Canadian schools. I think that is a phase of their activities that has not been mentioned in the house, but it is one of great importance. From their brief I notice that today there are thirty million young people throughout the world who are members of.junior Red Cross societies, and who are securing through that agency training in citizenship, personal health habits, social responsibility, and international amity.
With the world torn by factions as it is today, it is most encouraging to find that there is a voluntary organization comprising within its membership sixty-six nations of the world, an organization by means of which through its international conferences, international league and international committee, some sixty odd nations can get together and find a common basis of agreement. To me that is one of the great phases of Red Cross work, and certainly I will support any move that will strengthen this organization throughout the country.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the hon. member indicate now wherein this bill differs, if at all, from the bill passed by this house last session?

There is one slight
difference. The bill introduced last December had no limitation on the value of the real estate held in Canada. This bill has a limit of $200,000, which the society believes sufficient for their purposes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Was this limitation of $200,000 set out in the bill in the form in which the society asked that it be passed this year?
Yes.

My recollection of the bill of last year is that there was no limit on the value of the property. In this bill the $200,000 refers not to the value but to the annual value. Is there any difference there, in reality?

Perhaps it would be better if I gave one or two details of what the society means by "annual value". I refer to the resume, which I am sure all hon. members have received:
The general rise in real estate values and the extension of services has made it necessary that the limit on the annual value of the real estate which the society may hold under its present legislation he increased from $100,000 to $200,000 . . . Calculating the annual value at five per cent of the original purchase price or cost of construction, it will be seen that a limit of $200,000 would cover the real estate presently owned by the society and allow for some slight increase in its holdings.
It should be appreciated that "annual value," as far as the Canadian Red Cross Society holdings are concerned, is only an academic term, as no revenue is derived from such holdings and as many of the properties are so situated-for example, outpost hospitals-that it is unlikely that they would have either rental or sale value.

In connection with these bills I was interested to see in the Hardisty World a short article, part of which I shall read:
Alberta is having enough troubles these days deciding how best to make use of her great resources of natural gas, without having the situation messed up by Ottawa too. And that is just what is happening with the present filibuster going on in the nation's capital.
The article goes on to say:
What makes this all-Canada argument seem futile, at the present time at least, is that assurances have been given by a great many people that gas from Alberta will be guaranteed to British Columbia users before it is sold to Americans in the Pacific northwest. No one, of course, argues that the Americans are not going to get Alberta gas. Regardless of who builds a pipe line a great deal of the gas will have to be sold to U.S. cities. If it were not for the great gas market these cities are, there would be no pipe line because British Columbia alone does not represent a big enough market to justify building an expensive pipe line.
Then the hon. member for Calgary West made some remarks that I should like to place on Hansard. Speaking to the members of the Ottawa Gyro Club, he is reported as having said:
Emphasizing the urgent need for markets, Mr. Smith stated that 67,000 barrels of oil per day are being produced where 150,000 could be produced daily but there is nowhere to sell that amount. "That is one of the tragedies of this business," explained the speaker. . . .
The M.P. from the province that was "born lucky" explained that gas and oil are found together and so abundant is the latter that "enough gas to supply the needs of Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and all eastern Canada is being wasted in flares. If we had a market for our gas, we could continue our search for oil," said the speaker in conclusion.
Some of us in western Canada are particularly concerned that no misuse shall be made of this natural resource; and that if later on gas and oil are found in Saskatchewan or in the Peace river district of British Columbia, it will not be wasted or improperly used. We are not concerned, nor do I think most hon. members of this house are concerned, with any particular pipe line company. I do not know the representatives of these companies and have not been interviewed by them. I assume that applies to most of the members in this house. We are concerned, however, and deeply concerned in making sure that the people of Canada are first served with gas and oil. So far as the bill before the house is concerned, it applies to the building of a gas pipe line. The member for Calgary West says that there is an ample supply of
Alberta Natural Gas Company gas to fill the needs, not only of Canada but of the United States as well, for a great number of years.
We are not altogether satisfied with that assurance. I should like to discuss this afternoon the steps that have been taken to safeguard Canadian interests. I want to stress that the duty of protecting the public is purely a provincial duty. The natural resources in all these western provinces were handed back to the provinces by the federal government. They have full control of these resources, and tomorrow or any day can say that not one gallon of oil or one cubic foot of gas will be sold outside the province. The provincial government has that power, and having the power the duty devolves upon the provincial government.
Incidentally the government of Saskatchewan, which has allowed a large number of leases to be granted to people coming from Houston, Texas, and elsewhere, if gas or oil is discovered in large quantities, has a duty to safeguard the public. The provincial government can prohibit the export of gas or oil. What we are considering here is the matter of the safeguards for the public. Those of us who were born in the western provinces, and have lived there, are deeply interested in the welfare of those provinces. We have watched the freight rates, which I am not at liberty to discuss today because that matter is before a royal commission, and we have found that the western economy has been sadly impaired by the fixing of fictitious rates. I cannot go into detail about them today, but those of us who have studied the rates are convinced that is so.
In the province of Alberta alone we have a great supply of coal, water power, natural gas and oil, yet there are no large manufacturing concerns in that province such as are located in other parts of Canada. In the city of Winnipeg we have cheap hydro power, perhaps the cheapest on the North American continent. In spite of this there has been no development of industry. Western Canada will not be developed merely by letting this gas and oil go out all over the North American continent. We must first try to develop industries in the province of Alberta, the province of Manitoba, the city of Winnipeg and the other provinces. It is vital to our province that any governmental agency, whether it be provincial or federal, that has any control over the matter, exercise that control to ensure that these natural resources are not lost to the people of Canada.
We must now see what safeguards there are before this house. The matter of the immediate sale of this oil and gas is a mere bagatelle. It will give employment for a

Alberta Natural Gas Company short time, and it will give the people who hold the charters a great amount of money, but in the long run we may find as they did in Texas, Oklahoma, and the other states of the United States, that we have a bunch of dry holes and the communities are deserted because the industry has sold out all the gas and oil. We do not want that situation in the western provinces. We do not want our people to be forced to leave those provinces and migrate to the east or to British Columbia. If you are a bright lawyer now, you will go to the east or move to British Columbia and pay $1,500 for the privilege of entering a law practice. We do not want that situation in Canada. We look to the governmental agencies, particularly the provincial government that is in full control of these resources, to make sure that the people of the prairie provinces are taken care of first.	.
This bill that is before us is not a bill to fix a route. It is merely a bill to give the company a charter. It is being passed under the general Pipe Lines Act that was passed by a previous parliament, when many of the members who are sitting here today were not in attendance. As I pointed out in a previous debate, that bill was fostered and helped by those who are opposing this bill today. They were in favour of the initial bill that laid the groundwork for any private' bill. These members gave that initial bill full support. The only question today is which route should be chosen. I listened with a great deal of care to the member for Edmonton West the other evening, and I should like to congratulate him on his presentation. If it became a matter of a route, those in my constituency and those to the west of me in Saskatchewan would certainly favour the Yellowhead route. We cannot understand why the government of British Columbia, which endorsed a certain resolution favouring the Yellowhead route for the pipe line, did not endorse that route for the trans-Canada highway as well. It would have meant that the highway needed to protect the pipe line would have been built alongside of it. The British Columbia government picked another route entirely for the highway, and it goes through Banff; it does not touch Edmonton at all.
In this house we are concerned also with the welfare of the consumer in Canada, whether he is in British Columbia or elsewhere. I am not in favour of this house deciding; and whether the bill before the house is approved or rejected, we will not be deciding the route at all. It will simply


mean we are refusing one company a charter that we have granted to five other companies. Speaking again for the province of Saskatchewan, and I think possibly the Manitoba and Ontario members may take the same view, the bill that was before the house a year ago sponsored by the member for Fraser Valley concerning the West-coast Transmission Company did not even cover the provinces of Saskatchewan or Manitoba. It was only concerned with British Columbia and Alberta. It made no provision for furnishing gas or oil to any of the other provinces, whereas the bill before the house today applies to the whole of Canada.
And the United States.
And the United States.
First.
Not first; you are wrong there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I say again that if I were to speak in favour of any particular route, I would speak as the member for Edmonton West did, in favour of the Yellowhead route.
The attitude of the members opposed to this bill is not understandable to me. The member for Vancouver-Quadra is a lawyer, and a year ago in this house he spoke in high terms in favour of the general pipe lines bill. Yet in speaking in the debate in this house the other evening-
Last year I did say that it had to serve Canada first.

Let me point out to the minister that when that bill was put through the house-
That is the original pipe lines bill.
-last year there was not the slightest suggestion that the board of transport commissioners would have the power to decide whether or not a route to the west coast should go through the United States.

A company operating a company pipe line from a place in Canada to a place on the international boundary line may exercise, beyond such boundary, in so far as permitted by the laws there in force, the powers that it may exercise in Canada.

The

The bill then in connection with the West coast Transmission Company Is in exactly the same wording as this bill.
They guaranteed that an all-Canadian route would be built.
There was no guarantee whatever of anything.
Yes, there was.
There was nothing in that bill mentioning an all-Canadian route; and no guarantee of any sort was given.
A guarantee was given.

Now the hon. member comes to this house and says: "I want you to take my word for it that this company ten days ago told me that they would withdraw their application, or have done so, to build in the United States; and they withdrew it." There is nothing in the world, legally or otherwise, to prevent that company from re-applying for that route. There is nothing to prevent any one of the five companies you did incorporate- from transferring to any American company that they want to transfer to, taking their money and selling out the public even as these two pipe lines are doing. That is correct.
In addition, you also have on the statute books of Canada an act known as the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. In connection with that, no person can export oil or gas without the permission of an order in council which is put through by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That was on the statute books long before this pipe line bill. It is still on the statute books. What I am pointing out is that we have responsible government in Canada. If at any time there is danger of that field being used to excess, or the gas going to the wrong places, there is that power with the government of Canada. Also under the Pipe Lines Act, the board cf transport commissioners have the power to refuse a licence. If they refuse, the company cannot do business.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that in his opinion the board of transport commissioners was a fine board and would do a good job. He appreciated the

fact that the government had set up a board with power to pass on these things. He said that in the debate a year ago.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, you have a further safeguard in the persons of the government of the province of Alberta. I as a western member would call upon that government to make sure that there is no exploitation of this field, and that we do use as much of that gas and oil in Canada as can possibly be used here before the people of the United States get any of it.
In a previous debate the hon. member for Calgary West had a great deal to say about the conservation board of Alberta. He said that that board was amply seized of the whole situation. He said they were smart people who knew all about it. He praised them to the skies and said he was quite satisfied with the Alberta conservation board. This was said by an hon. member who has been opposing these bills. When the bill went through last year he praised the board and said he was satisfied with it.
Now let us see what the government of the province of Alberta has to say about it. Let us see what safeguards they give us. Just bear in mind that the law is quite clear, as laid down by the Prime Minister in the same debate. In effect he said that the government of the province of Alberta alone can export oil out of Alberta, and they have full control over it. He said:
I cannot change the constitution. In my view the resources of a province are controlled by the legislation of that province. If there is legislation in the province of Alberta saying that the owners of fields where there is gas must comply with regulations made by a board set up under the authority of that legislation, I think as a lawyer they would have to do so, because that is control of property and civil rights within the province. The federal government has the right to control export but it cannot force export. It cannot say that property belonging to the hon. member shall be taken from him and exported.
The laws relating to the hon. member's property are under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, but if it is something that is free to be dealt with the federal government can say, notwithstanding that it is free to be dealt with, "We will not give you a permit to export it unless you comply with such and such regulation."
If there is any doubt as to what these companies are going to do the government of Canada could pass regulations, either under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act or under the present act, and enforce them, but the first duty is the province's. The hon. member for Calgary West says that the conservation board in Alberta is an intelligent one. So, there are your protections, and a lot of the talk that has been going on in this holise I submit is far away from the point. We are not deciding a route. If we had to decide a route, as the Prime Minister has so
Alberta Natural Gas Company ably stated, we would have to go into all the details. We do not want to build a pipe line around every valley in British Columbia in order to give service. We want to build it in an economical way so that the consumers will not have to pay too much for the pipe line and too high a price for their gas and oil. That is the situation. It can only be gone into and carefully examined by the board of transport commissioners. I had their names available a while ago, but I have mislaid them. One of the members is a former premier of my province, Mr. Patterson. I believe they have a representative from British Columbia, and there are three other other members. Judge Archibald of Nova Scotia is the chairman. Under the act constituting the board they have, the power to examine the applications before any permission is given to export. There is the maximum of protection under the electricity and fluid act to which I referred a moment ago. Therefore there are these two protections as far as the federal government is concerned.
All this talk about Canada first should be directed first to the province of Alberta arid then to the governments of the other prairie provinces, and then to those other two bodies to which I have referred. As far as this house is concerned, to keep on arguing in this debate as to whether this company or that company is going to build a pipe line here or there is to my mind, Mr. Chairman, absolute nonsense, because we could never agree on a route any more than some provinces have agreed up to date on a trans-Canada highway route. We would have the same troubles that have cropped up there.

You still have ten
minutes.
I am glad to know that the hon. member for Fraser Valley is enjoying my remarks. I appreciate a good audience, and I know of his intelligence.
I want to know which United States route you favour.

May I say to the
hon. member that the only United States route I know of is the one mentioned in the bill he introduced. That is the only one we have seen in the house.
Your company advertised it.

So far as Saskatchewan is concerned, I have a letter from the commissioner of the board of trade of Saskatoon. We want protection in that province. We do not want it all to go to British Columbia. Sometimes you get some hon.

Alberta Natural Gas Company members from that province who take an allCanadian view, and at other times, when they get west of those mountains, they take a very narrow view. They are isolated on the west coast-
That is the Liberal-

There is another narrow view. I have even seen a broadminded Conservative at times. In any event the commissioner at Saskatoon said this:
The question was raised as to whether Saskatchewan's interests in getting supplies of gas for this province should not be protected. The thought was that, in any such bill authorizing the exportation of gas to centres in British Columbia, Saskatchewan's probable needs of natural gas should be provided for before any gas was exported to British Columbia.
Who has the narrow view now?
That is the view of the Saskatoon board of trade.
A narrow view.
But you want to hog everything for British Columbia. We could build a gas route much cheaper into Regina and Saskatoon than you can around the Rocky mountains.
What about Yorkton?

Yorkton will be reached ultimately, because all good things emanate around that city; even the Minister of Agriculture comes from near there. I continue with the letter:
Fear was expressed that, if the private bill passed the House of Commons providing for the construction of a pipe line to bring gas to British Columbia, a future bill requesting the construction of a pipe line to bring gas into Saskatchewan might be refused on the ground that there was not sufficient gas in Alberta to supply the needs of both pipe lines.
I was instructed to bring this matter to your attention with the request that your department consider fully the consequences which may flow from the passage of the private bill in question.
That is the position of the Saskatoon board of trade. You cannot blame them for taking that attitude, when you take the attitude of a sponsor of that bill in this house-and I am now referring to the hon. member for Fraser Valley.

which ignores the province of Saskatchewan, that beautiful province, and the province of Manitoba-
Most people from Saskatchewan have moved to British Columbia.

I know, and at one
time there was objection to that from some of your narrow-minded people. You did not want immigration from Saskatchewan, at one time, and you had to apologize.
Who said that?

You just want selective
immigration.
You remember the controversy which took place in the Vancouver papers about that.
We did not want too many from Yorkton.
Since the westerners got out there with their western breezes you have wakened up quite a bit. That is all I wish to say on this bill at this time.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Yorkton has given us quite a scolding. After hearing what the Prime Minister said on Friday night I somehow thought that scolding was off, but we are back at it again because the hon. member has told us that this is all a tempest in a teapot, it is a filibuster. But then, as I understood him, he tried to indicate that he was really of one mind with those who wished to see the construction done in the Dominion of Canada. I could not help feeling at the end of the hon. member's speech that he was somewhat in the position of a man who was described to me some time ago, as a man who was ready to give all aid short of help. It seems to me that that is where we are.
When I made a few opening remarks the other night I said that I rose to my feet because I had a feeling, which I believe was widely shared in this house, that this bill was not what it seemed to be, that under the guise of being a private bill it was not so very private. I felt that the government, or at any rate some members of the government, or at least one member of the government, had a lot more to do with it than we were really allowed to know. I think this has become a matter of considerable public interest and I should like to read a sentence or two from Saturday Night which is not regarded as being partisan of the party I am associated with. Speaking of this matter Saturday Night says:
Here Is a question of deep-rooted principles. In spite of all the opposition's attempts the government has so far refused to debate it in the House of Commons.
Since that time the Prime Minister has spoken. Saturday Night continues:
It looks like being settled in the secret conclaves of the board of transport commissioners and the cabinet. We think it would be a pity if the house let that happen: the Canadian public have some concern in the matter.
I think that expresses very well the feelings of a great number of people as well as members of this house. I think we are entitled and have been entitled to carry on this debate. On Friday night the Prime

Minister took quite a different tone from what has been taken by those associated with him, and I shall have occasion to refer in some detail to what he said.
I have always hoped, and I think others of my mind have as well, that these charters might be granted. We believe that the Alberta government is quite right in saying that it wants to have more than one applicant available. That has always been said by the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, but they contended that the charters should be granted on proper terms. That is also what was said the other night by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano.
Before I forget, I must say that the attitude which characterized the proceedings in the committee was not what it should have been. Hon. members will recall that we were urged to let this bill go to the committee when, as was represented, we could get all the information which was desirable and necessary and where the matter could be discussed. I shall have occasion later to describe what actually happened in that committee which certainly was a travesty of what we were invited to expect.
I should like now to put on record just what the Prime Minister actually did say, and I do this in the light of all the talk there has been about filibustering, which the hon. member for Yorkton has reiterated. The hon. member and the Prime Minister ought to have a caucus on this. I quote from page 2229 of Hansard of May 5, 1950-
The hon. member is out of order in referring to another debate.
I will wait until the chairman calls me to order.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. That ruling seems to me to be one which is eminently filled with common sense, but whether it will coincide with the hon. member's views as to technicalities, I do not know. This is what the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 2229 of Hansard:
I am not going to suggest that the protracted debates in this parliament about the desirability of an all-Canadian pipe line for the gas and oil of 55946-144
Alberta Natural Gas Company
Alberta have been a waste of time. It has aroused public opinion as to the desirability of doing that if it is possible. I would expect that that would not be lost from the point of view of the members of the board of transport commissioners and that they would not lightly disregard the unanimous desire of Canadians that their own territory be used to the greatest possible advantage.
I stress those words "unanimous desire of Canadians". I would think the board of transport commissioners might pay considerable attention to what the Prime Minister said. Whether he should have said it is another matter. At any rate it makes it more likely that what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and others have been fighting for will in the end come about, but my concern is that it should not only come about but come about in the right way.
In order to give this committee an idea of the proper atmosphere of this debate it is desirable for us to recall that after all hon. members of this house have certain rights and privileges. One privilege is for the minority to debate. It is not for any member of this house to decide when the point is reached when the minority is to stop debating, except under the rules of the house. There have been plenty of cases where minorities have ended up by being majorities, and I refer now to particular enactments where public opinion had had time to catch up. It looks to me as if public opinion was catching up here, judging from some of the things that have happened in this house already.
I should like to go back to what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on November 15, 1949, and I quote from page 1807 of Hansard of that date:
I should like also to say a word about what seems obviously to be a filibuster in connection with these bills. The government will not permit any small number of members to prevent this house as a whole from voting on a private bill.
I think we should ponder that. What was really meant was that the government was not going to allow private members to exercise the right which they have. That is what was intended to be said. I continue:
If these bills continue to be talked out in the limited time permitted for private bills, the government will ask the house to suspend the rules and provide whatever time is required to finish the discussion and to obtain a vote on such bills.
One would think that a crime was being committed, yet I think it is within the experience of us all that the talking out of private bills has been indulged in by the government or by government representatives. We have seen what happened here in the case of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Resources and Development, who is really a man of distinction in that respect. He acted as a kind of shock trooper, and I suppose it
2268	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company might not be irrelevant to suggest that that brought him some political preferment. I am not objecting particularly to that being done; I am only saying that it works both ways.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce said what he did to the house he said something which was quite improper, and something which in fact produced a result quite different from what was expected. I very much doubt, if he had not said what he did say, whether there would have been nearly as much debate as has occurred since. But he was not the only one. The Prime Minister had something to say about that, though it is quite true the Prime Minister did not put it quite as crudely as the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Prime Minister is a man of more-what shall I say?-delicacy of expression than the Minister of Trade and Commerce, although at times he can be delicate if he wants to. Here is what the Prime Minister said, and I quote from page 1999 of Hansard of November 21, 1949:
The bills In question have been before the house on four occasions-
A terrible thing. I wonder if there are not members of this house who can recall certain bills which they wanted to get through and which were talked out more often than four times. I continue:
-during the hour reserved for private bills, and on each of those occasions the time allotted proved to be too short-
What a pity.
-to permit of an expression of opinion by the house.
Then here is what is really a model of understatement:
It would perhaps be the feeling of hon. members that there should be an opportunity to permit of a decision being made by the house.
That is just another way of saying what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said. The Prime Minister did provide extra time, so there you have them working together hand in hand toward the same end and seeking to disregard the rights of the minority in this house. Since then we have had the Prime Minister's speech, from which I read you the sentence a moment or two ago in which he said, speaking of this debate, "it has aroused public opinion". I should like to ask if there is any more useful purpose which a debate in this house can serve than to arouse public opinion on a matter in which the public is interested.
I am glad that the Prime Minister has come to that view. After all, this house does not exist merely so that those who are not members of the government-and I speak now of all private members, not merely of
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

those who ordinarily vote against the government-shall just be rubber stamps. Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce came very near reaching that point. I think there was genuine surprise when there was a really firm attempt to stop this legislation going through. I think we have drifted along to that point in this house. The government does not want to do away with the opposition because that would give the whole show away if the opposition were not there. The public would then begin to prick up their ears if they saw that they were getting a one-party state. The government want to have the opposition but they want it to be tame. The opposition can make speeches and oppose but it must never do anything very much.
When a determined stand was taken on these measures I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister obviously were scandalized. They had not seen it happen often before and they did not like it. Indeed, I suppose this is probably one of the most successful efforts that have been made to let public opinion catch up, as it were. Public opinion is often difficult to arouse. The ordinary citizen has not got as much time as we have to study and familiarize himself with these questions, but this was a case where he was given some time and where he seems to have made quite a job. It almost, seems as if public opinion had invaded the Liberal caucus, if we are to believe the newspaper article that the Prime Minister read to us the other day, although he finally had to tell us of course that it was all wrong. No-he did not actually say it was wrong. He merely said that it was not a thing that one talked about. In a moment I propose to read just what he said.
From what the Prime Minister said it is clear that it is quite respectable now to take part in this debate. I am sorry that the hon. member for Yorkton seemed to think that it was not but the Prime Minister has really made it respectable. I think we should be rather grateful to him for that because, as I say, it looks as though public opinion had even got as far as the Liberal caucus.
I should now like to say a word about what the Prime Minister said in the house on Friday night. He explained that he had not been intending to take part in the debate but his mind had been changed by reason of a news story in the Montreal Gazette. He went on to say at page 2227 of Hansard:
This newspaper story is at page 11 of today's issue, and bears the title, "Gardiner Said To Be Demanding All-Canadian Pipe Lines Route."
It is very interesting to us to hear that. We all take a great interest in the views of the Minister of Agriculture, and of course we all

hope this is true. I imagine this is one occasion when the Minister of Agriculture may not interrupt me, although he nearly always does.
I never discuss caucus out of caucus.

I understand that nobody is supposed to do that but it would appear as though people often do. Then the Prime Minister went on with rather extraordinarily well chosen words because as I read his words you will see that he did not say that anything reported in the article had not happened. He really just said to talk about it out of caucus was not the kind of thing that was done; at any rate it was not talked about in public. Here is what he said:
Now, all hon. members know that the deliberations of party caucuses are confidential, just as are the deliberations of council.
I must say I think \he deliberations of council are more confidential than those of party caucuses, but I think it is perhaps a strong statement in either case. The Prime Minister continued:
I am quite sure that no one who attended that caucus ever informed anyone outside of party members of anything that transpired within the walls of the hall where it was held.
I should like to think that was true, Mr. Chairman, but I find very great difficulty in believing it is, and perhaps you do also. The Prime Minister went on to say:
So the whole story about what goes on in our caucus, just as any story about what goes on in the caucuses of any other of the parties, must be the writer's guesswork in that respect.
Then he said something with which we will all agree. He said:
He would not expect me, I am sure, and no one else would expect me to say anything here about what went on in that caucus, either by way of confirmation or by way of denial.
I think that is a very fair statement. I do not think we would expect the Prime Minister to say that, but there you have it. We have this indication, as I say, that public opinion has got into the caucus. We may never know if public opinion has had this extraordinary effect on the Minister of Agriculture except in so far as we can judge by his actions. It would certainly appear as if public opinion had had an effect upon the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. It would appear as if he, like Joan of Arc, had heard voices and as if those voices had had considerable effect on him.
I think that is all to the good. That is public opinion at work; that is what this debate has brought about in spite of the deliberate attempt of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to silence the minority. He does not 55946-144J
Alberta Natural Gas Company think much of debates. I am sorry he is not here. I always like to have him here. I do not know where he is. Perhaps he is off making another trade treaty, and we may have another statement in the morning telling us that everything is O.K. At any rate I wish he were here because I always like his interruptions.
I should like to say a word about the proceedings before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I want to read what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in that regard because his point was that if we would only send these things to the committee all would be well. The minister said that we were most unreasonable in trying to keep these measures away from the committee. At page 1806 of Hansard for November 15, 1949, he said:
However, I do think that these acts should be studied and studied very carefully. I should like to know much more about the incorporation asked for in the bill about which I am speaking than I know at the present time. But the place to obtain that information is in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to which this bill will be referred, and before which the sponsors of the bill will appear to make their case for incorporation.
At the moment, that sounded quite persuasive to me, and I had great difficulty in not accepting that view. Indeed we have had a similar view expressed to us this afternoon rather persuasively by the hon. member for Yorkton when he described to us all these other boards-and they do exist

whose permission must be obtained. As I thought further about the matter however it seemed to me that none of that was an excuse for parliament giving a blank cheque and disregarding our own responsibility. If you remember what happens in the case of the railways, my information is that the board of transport commissioners is limited in its powers, that it has no wide-open power to give permission for the construction of long stretches of railway. I believe their power is limited to six miles, and that the power to do anything beyond that has always been vested in and exercised by this house.
Dealing with the question of the committee, there are one or two features which are rather interesting. Of course the star member of the committee was the parliamentary assistant who took a very definite line in the committee from the outset. He did not think much of the idea of information being given in the committee. In the early stages of the proceedings on the bill he told us that he did not know anything about it, and he evidently felt that nobody else needed to know anything about it either.

What parliamentary
assistant?

Alberta Natural Gas Company

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I should like to read a few excerpts from the proceedings of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines of April 27 because other members apparently were quite ready to have the information given although the parliamentary assistant felt differently about it. At the very beginning of the meeting Mr. Prudham said:
I would then like to move that the chairman he empowered to call additional witnesses to give evidence as to route.
Apparently that indicated a change of heart on the part of Mr. Prudham because during the proceedings of April 26 Mr. Prudham said:
I think it is entirely out of order for us to discuss routes in this committee. But if we are going to discuss routes, then all routes should be discussed, including other routes which are not covered by the survey of this company.
While I do not agree with the first proposition I think his second one perhaps is right. So on Thursday morning the hon. member for Edmonton West said:
I would then like to move that the chairman be empowered to call additional witnesses to give evidence as to route.
A little later the hon. member for Tnvemess-Richmond said:
... I am sure there would be only one question that X would be interested in and that is the question of route. . . .
That seems reasonable enough so far, but here is what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had to say:
Mr. Chairman, I think that if we bring in any more witnesses in reference to routes we will only waste more time and I do not think that the route question is germane to this bill.
Then certain other questions were asked; the hon. member for Yancouver-Quadra did not entirely agree, and indicated his disagreement, suggesting that the statement as to wasting time should be withdrawn. The chairman, evidently wishing to pour oil on the troubled waters, said:
I see no objection to the withdrawal of it.
But the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre replied:
There is no objection to its being withdrawn excepting that I shall not withdraw it.
That was very clear. A little later, however, he changed his mind; he does change his mind at times. He said:
I think X have a right to say it. However, we will get along with this matter this way: merely to advance the action, I will withdraw it. It is on the record, though.
Apparently the chairman did not altogether like that. He said:
I do not think we will get further along like this.

Then the hon. member for Winnipeg Soutn Centre said:
I do not know just how one does manage to make statements and have them withdrawn. It is on the record and the people who have heard it will, no doubt, continue to be influenced by it, some one way, and some another.
Hon. members can take that and make what they like of it. What I make of it is that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was seeking in every way to have the committee prevented from doing what we in this house were assured it was set up to do. However, that committee was very useful in one way, because it did enable a check-up to be made of a step that had been taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who had tried to help matters along by writing a letter to the Vancouver city council on April 4, in which he said:
While it is alleged that the Alberta Natural Gas Company, if incorporated, proposes to build a pipe line through the United States, this is not the information that the company has given me. My information is that the new company is proposing to build its lines through all-Canadian territory and to serve all Vancouver points before taking the line into the United States.
In examining Mr. Dixon, the chief witness for the company, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked about this very point:
Q. Will you give any pledge to this committee that your company, if it is incorporated, will build the Canada-first line, build a main line through Canada to the west coast?
A. No.
Q. Mr. Dixon, that is clear-cut and we are glad to have that statement, but I ask you if in your talks with the Right Honourable Mr. Howe, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that is the stand you have taken?
A. Just exactly. I have not said anything to Mr. Howe that I have not said to you.
Q. Mr. Howe wrote a letter to the Vancouver city council on April 4 of this year, in which he said-
That is the part I read.
Now, you dispute that, the terms of that'letter by Mr. Howe?
A. I told him just what I told you, that we had the five routes, that we would build any line we would be permitted to build, that the board of transport commissioners told us that we would be permitted to build. If the board of transport commissioners tells us to build the all-Canadian route that will be the line that will be built.
Q. Did you assure Mr. Howe that you were going to build an all-Canadian route?
A. I wish we could have assured him that we were going to build any line.
Q. So you did not assure him you were going to build an all-Canadian route?
A. Well, we said we would build an all-Canadian route if the board of transport commissioners selected it. He was perfectly correct in his statement.
Q. If you were ordered?
A. If we were ordered.

So we have this curious action on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I think it is very simple to explain. I think when the minister feels something has to be done, as far as he is concerned it is done; and, if it is done, why not say so? Sometimes I think that involves him in slight inaccuracies and optimistic statements. I think anyone looking at this record will realize that far from having given the minister any assurance that they would do what he said, all the applicants for the charter said was that they would do what they were ordered.
I could go further in speaking about the proceedings before this committee, but I do not think I need take time for that. There was constant unwillingness to give time, and at the last the committee was shut off by a resolution. I had never reflected upon it adequately before, but one of the things that struck me was that when you go from this committee of the whole to a committee of the house the minority loses all its rights. It is then subject only to the will of the majority, however high-handed; and I think anyone who reads those reports, as I have read them, will agree that when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said the minority in this committee had been dealt with in a highhanded manner, he was making what the other evening I termed a conservative statement.
I do not intend to devote any time to the matter of route; I think that has been dealt with by people better qualified than I. But there is one thing I believe should be said. A very considerable number of hon. members have expressed their views as to routes, including the hon. member for York-ton. A good deal has been said about the advantages of the Yellowhead route; but, to put it mildly, I think it was rather astonishing when the chief witness for this company, Mr. Dixon, admitted quite candidly that his only knowledge of the Yellowhead route was gained on a trip through it by train, though he had studied the other routes carefully. As the hon. member for Kootenay West pointed out the other evening, a very significant statement was made by Mr. Dixon when he said they had ordered some 400 miles of pipe. On studying the map the hoh. member discovered that this was exactly the quantity required to take the pipe line to the United States border. That was interesting in two ways. It showed that while Mr. Dixon professed to be perfectly ready to build over whatever route they were ordered to build, nevertheless they were so sure in their own minds, and apparently so convinced
Alberta Natural Gas Company that they were going to get their own way, that according to him they had ordered these 400 miles of pipe.
At the outset I said my reason for taking part in this debate is that I consider the House of Commons has been very shabbily treated in this matter. I believe there is a widespread feeling here that far from being a private bill this is in effect a public measure. I should like to refer to the words used the other evening by the Prime Minister, because they were rather interesting. A writer in the Gazette had said, as appears at page 2227 of Hansard:
The high degree of interest in these reports out of caucus stems from the fact that, up to the present, the government had made it plain that it felt that parliament should give the two companies a free hand in selecting the route along which they would build the huge pipe line.
The Prime Minister dealt with that on page 2228 in these words:
I do not know what the companies have made plain. I did not attend the meetings of the committees, I have not seen any of the promoters of these companies. I have not read the testimony taken in committee, nor the report of the committee.
It is rather a pity the Prime Minister did not read those proceedings; he might have had his eyes opened.
I do know that if anyone in the press gallery had come to the conclusion that the government had made it plain that it felt that parliament should give the two companies a free hand to select the route along which they would build the huge pipe line, others may have reached the same conclusion, and I feel I am called upon to point out that there was no such thing made plain by the government, nor ever intended to be made plain by the government.
It will be observed that those are very carefully chosen words. I would have to agree that it had not been made plain, and my whole complaint about this business is that nothing has been made plain. We are left to inferences, which we would much rather not have to make in certain cases. But the hon. member supported the route through the United States, and voted for it.
