I never supported any route through the United States. I did support the idea of incorporating this company, because I think in Canada there should be free competition. These people promoted a company and they have come to parliament to ask for incorporation. Who am I to deny them that right? It is not proper to make a monopoly in this industry, and I do not propose to subscribe to it.
There is another important angle to the proposal that the line should be carried down through the Cariboo. The Canadian National Railways line runs from Jasper to the riding of my friend the member for Skeena, and that part of the line is not very profitable, although it services that part of the country. I believe the Canadian National is in the red possibly about $35 million a year. Would it not be in the public interest to promote trade and development along the Canadian National railway line in that area? The development of these natural resources would mean that more tonnage could be carried by the Canadian National railway to Prince Rupert on the west or eastward to Edmonton. It is of interest to the people of Canada, not merely the people of British Columbia, to make the Canadian National Railways prosperous. The building of a pipe line through that area, stimulating the activity of those industries,. would be of direct benefit to the Canadian National Railways.
There is a much more important local angle to it than that in British Columbia. We have the Pacific Great Eastern Railway running up through that country that I have mentioned. At the last session we made to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway a subvention of approximately $2 million, to assist them in building from Quesnel to Prince George. The plans in British Columbia are to extend that railroad into the Peace river country. What better arrangement could you have than to have it running along or near the main pipe line conveying the oil and gas from the interior of northern Alberta and British Columbia to the Pacific coast? That is a project that will figure prominently in discussions in the future. I know that members of the legislature of British Columbia submitted a resolution on it, and I know that in drawing up that resolution they had in
Alberta Natural Gas Company mind the salvaging of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and the great investment of British Columbia in Cariboo, in Peace river and in that northern part of British Columbia. I would not be surprised to see this subject, which is now before this committee and is taking up so much time, become a prominent question in the next provincial election in British Columbia; and I hope that I shall be spared to be there to have an important part in the discussions.
You had better talk differently than you have been talking so far.
He has a new speech now.
Because I was broadminded enough to agree to the incorporation of this second company and this third company, you suggest that I want to build a pipe line through the United States.
Sure you would.

You do not know British Columbia. You do not know the mountains of British Columbia as I do. You do not know those mountain passes. Do you know why those fantastic routes have been placed before you? It is a political idea, to featherstitch that pipe line to as many ridings as possible for political reasons. There are certain places where it will be cheap to build a pipe line. Those passes in the north are much more accessible than the passes to the south. That is known to everybody who knows the mountains of British Columbia. The Peace river pass is broad and low and it would be easy to build a pipe line through there; and of course it would be a simple matter to do the same north of Prince George to the Peace river. Peace river is very accessible, and it would be a simple matter to lay a pipe line in there. The same is true of the Yellowhead pass. As you go north, I can tell you that these passes are lower and more accessible, and any sensible engineer would tell you that.
There is just one weakness in that whole set-up and that is that they have not surveyed the various routes that we have been talking about. We know they have not surveyed the Yellowhead. Everybody admits it. Since it was brought up by the hon. member for Fraser Valley and others, there has been snow in the Yellowhead. You could not have sent engineers up there since last October anyway, to do any good in the Yellowhead. I doubt if they spent much money in these other explorations.
Of course, you have the engineering data of the railways. You know the altitudes and so on and so forth. But this is a big project. There are many millions of dollars at stake

Alberta Natural Gas Company with regard to the oil in western Canada. I am sorry that at the committee, when I suggested bringing in Mr. T. Link, an authority on this subject, objection was made. When I wanted to bring in Mr. Stanley Slipper, who is a great geologist and who knows all about the work which has already been accomplished there, objection was made to that. I hope that these men and others will be brought before the board of transport commissioners, and I hope the board of transport commissioners will not only accept some route which is suggested to them but that they will lay down and decide which route will be taken in conveying this great resource from central Canada to the Pacific coast.
I have said what I wished to say on this matter. I hope that this bill will pass. I hope that we in the House of Commons shall not do anything to discourage the investment of American capital in this country. I would point out to the committee that the development of the oil and natural gas in Alberta and northern British Columbia has been done largely by American capital. We have had some examples of Canadian financiers who have vision and enterprise like my good friend Major James Lowery of Home Oil; but our Canadians are much in the minority in the development of that great resource in Alberta. It is time we woke up and took a little keener interest in the industry. There is no reason why we should call on any American company to build any route. We have here the money, the material, the men and the ability to carry this thing out for ourselves.
I will just close my speech with this remark. It has been said that Joan of Arc heard voices. I would say that some of our members here heard voices since they first voted on these things and the voices caused them to vote in a direction opposite to that which was indicated. I am prepared to make a little prophecy and it is that the final route for the construction of the pipe line will be through Cariboo, through central British Columbia to the city of Vancouver, and from that point on to two and a half million people in the state of Washington; and to the great industry at Trail and to the other industries which will provide some market for the surplus oil and gas of this country.
Before I close I want to point with regret to the fact that so much gas and oil are being wasted today in those western fields. Not long ago I was in Leduc, and at every producing gas well, flames were flaring high in the air burning off what was said to be waste material. All I can say is that it was waste material that certainly would


not have been wasted in an American oil field. It was gas going to waste. I was up at Peace River crossing in the riding of the hon. member for Athabaska, or is it of the hon. member for Peace River? There is there an eight-inch gas pipe which has been burning, to my personal knowledge, for twenty-five years, the flame going high into the heavens, burning this gas.
Rome burned while Nero fiddled; and gas enough to light and heat Montreal and Ottawa together is going to waste while hon. members of this House of Commons are fiddling here, filibustering, discussing and debating over what they are going to do about it.

I do not think anybody in the committee can accuse me of filibustering, Mr. Chairman. This is only the second time I have spoken on any of these bills; and I would not have been long if I had not been interrupted a great deal when I last spoke. I hope 1 will not get quite so much interference this time.
Following the hon. member for Cariboo, may I say that I can quite understand that he really knows the area out in that country, as he has. described it quite fully. But I am surprised at his speaking now, as I would say, in favour of an all-Canadian route; because in the committee, he was one of the members who had quite a lot to say, and many questions to ask, but when the vote came, he voted for an American route.
Every time.
Yes, every time.
That is not so.
That is a fact, and you cannot deny it.

I voted against petty motions that were brought in with the idea of endlessly delaying the discussion and keeping this bill from a vote in the House of Commons. I voted against filibustering in the committee.

No such thing. You voted for an American route every time, as the record will show.
In my last speech, on April 3, before Easter, I moved the adjournment of the debate. At page 1501 of Hansard I said in effect that I thought it would be well to adjourn the debate and leave it over until after the Easter recess so that hon. members could go home and talk to their constituents, which would give them a little more time to decide just what they were debating.
It was a good idea.

I believe it had some effect, because since that time we have had hon. members who were in favour of the bill at that time now taking the same attitude as I am. No matter how smart we think we are as members of parliament, there are times when we can go to some fellow in the back concession and get a lot of information from him which would be valuable to us.
Other hon. members have come around to our way of thinking. One of these is the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, one of my keen interrupters on the day I made my speech. However, he has had a change of mind and of heart.
He has seen the light.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked for that.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was endeavouring to complete my remarks on this pipe line bill. I was being interrupted by an hon. member who is not present at the moment. Perhaps that is just as well as I can finish a little more quickly. Since these pipe line bills have been before us there has been no evidence at all offered that a line directly through Canada would be built. It is only the one company that has already received a charter that has said definitely it would build over a Canadian route through the Yellowhead pass.
I think it was the hon. member for Edmonton West who said that the Yellowhead pass was accessible. I assume that he knows more about that than I. The Canadian National Railways runs through that pass and we would probably use our own government system in building a pipe line over this route. Some one has said that it will be necessary to build a highway alongside the pipe line. So much the better. Another road would be built through British Columbia which would probably attract tourist business to that area. I happen to live in a place that has been built up largely through the tourist business and I know something about it. If this road will create tourist business it will probably prove to be one of the best paying roads in Canada. Such a road would build up the cities and towns of that province industrially and commercially and more business would be created for our Canadian railroads as well as for the highway itself.

If this road is built and people decide to go into the tourist business you will have thousands of tourists coming up from the United States to view our scenery. These tourists can look at the same scenery as often as they like and it is never depleted. Scenery is not like a mine or a timber limit or anything like that which is gradually depleted; our scenery will be there for all time provided we protect it properly. You can use it as much as you like and there is no wearing out.
If this pipe line goes through British Columbia the towns and cities will be built up. British Columbia has the ore, the timber and all the natural resources to build up many industries. If cheap power and heat are available the development there will be an asset to the whole country. I know that if there were any chance of having this pipe line go through my riding I would be saying a lot more than I have. I would be working as hard as possible to get that pipe line run through my own riding or even close to it.
There must be a lot of money in the operation of pipe lines. One bill has gone through the house, another is in process of being put through, and another is to follow. The chances are there will be two or three more companies applying for charters. It is stated that the difference in cost between one route and the other is somewhere between $15 million and $17 million. That is a lot of money and it may involve considerable pressure on the board of transport commissioners. I submit that this matter should be settled in the House of Commons by the elected representatives of the people.
The Canadian National Railways is an organization already in existence and for the life of me I cannot see why this pipe line could not be built by that organization. At the present time the Canadian National Railways has a deficit of $42 million. Apparently everyone wants to build a pipe line. One of the engineers said it was like a horse race, it was a matter of who got there first. Why could not this pipe line be built by the Canadian National Railways and thus give a chance to balance that $42 million deficit in the years to come, from the profits from the pipe lines? The Canadian Pacific shows more profits from the operations of its other projects than it does from the operations of the railroad.
Is the hon. member talking about nationalization?

You can go a certain extent in nationalizing things as long as it is not socialization. We have a number of examples in our own country. In Ontario there is the

hydro and we have the Canadian National Railways. There are many other projects, such as Polymer, which I mentioned the other evening. I think there is a lot of money to be made out of a pipe line.
Before this bill is passed the government engineers should survey the Yellowhead route and make a report on what it would cost to build the pipe line. It would not hurt to hold up this bill for another couple of months because it is not a killing matter. One hon. member said that they had been burning gas out there for twenty-five years but surely in another month there would not be much more wasted. If this route could be examined by government engineers probably an argument could be put forth that the pipe line should be built by the Canadian National Railways.
I do not think there was any doubt in the minds of all hon. members of the committee from the evidence given by Mr. Dixon that there was only one route they intended to follow, the one through the United States. Any hon. member of that committee who listened to the whole proceedings could come to no other conclusion. The engineers could offer no figures in connection with the Yellow-head pass, but they said they could get them. If they can get them, so can the government. I think that should be done before we go any further.
We have been selling our natural resources to the United States for a long time and it is time to call a halt. We should start to use these natural resources in Canada for the benefit of Canada as a whole. It does not matter whether an industry is built up in the east or the west, it is of benefit to Canada. I do not think I have anything more to say and as far as I am concerned the vote can be taken any time. But I would like to see this held over so that the government engineers could go out and look over that area.

Mr. Chairman, this is the second time I have spoken on these pipe line bills in the two sessions they have been before the house. I want to speak tonight for a few moments as a member of the committee to which these measures were sent. First of all I want to register, along with other members, my protest against the way in which, in my opinion, the bills were railroaded through the committee. As you know, the Monday of the week on which the bills came before the committee was taken away from us as a private member's day, and the first full private member's day was the Monday following the week on which these bills reached the standing committee.

It soon became quite apparent to members of the committee that there was a well organized group of Liberal members on it with the full intention of getting the bills back into the house on the following Monday. We have in the trade union movement a name for people who do the kind of work that I felt Liberal members of the committee were doing. In trade union language we call them hatchet men. In the very early stages of the sittings of the committee there was a determined effort to prevent the committee from considering routes at all. An attempt was made to point out that that was not the purpose of the committee although we had been told on numerous occasions in the house that the whole purpose of sending the bills to the committee was to secure all relevant information concerning the matter.
Then of course there was the attempt to protect the witness whenever any question was raised that proved embarrassing either to the witness or to the supporters of the bill. An onlooker would have thought that many members of the committee were there for the express purpose of protecting the interests of the company whose witness was before the committee. A deliberate effort was made and closure applied to prevent the committee from calling witnesses. A number of members asked for witnesses but if the bills were to be before the house again on the following Monday there was not time to call witnesses who could have given us much relevant information.
I have been a member of a number of committees of the house, and I think I can say quite frankly that this committee was the most political of any in whose proceedings I have taken part.

I want to compliment the witness, Mr. Dixon, who appeared for the company. He gave us every evidence of being quite familiar with his field and he was quite frank. He told us frankly that he had given the Minister of Trade and Commerce no assurance that his company would build an all-Canadian line notwithstanding a letter to that effect which was put on the record of the committee. He stated quite clearly to us that his company was not prepared to have a clause inserted in the bill calling for an all-Canadian route. When asked bluntly if his company would consent to the inclusion of such a clause in the bill he frankly told us "No". I think he clearly showed his personal preference, and his company's preference, for an all-American route. He did that by pointing out to us the many disadvantages of an all-Canadian route. He frankly showed

Alberta Natural Gas Company us that an all-Canadian route would take one year longer to build than an all-American route. He told us quite frankly that the allCanadian route would cost $17,000 a mile more to build, or a total of $17 million on a route of approximately 1,000 miles.
He told us quite frankly that the Canadian route would be more costly to maintain, and that people on the Canadian west coast would pay more for their gas if it were piped by an all-Canadian route than by an all-American route. He said quite frankly that his company had given consideration to only one Canadian route while they had studied four wholly or partially United States routes. Of the five routes submitted, only one was allCanadian. One was practically all-American and the other three to a large extent were United States routes. No evidence was given before the committee to show that his company had been concerned with finding the most economical Canadian route. Some statements were made by other members of the committee indicating that Canadian routes other than the one outlined by Mr. Dixon would possibly be more economical or would serve Canada better. The witness frankly admitted that his company had only been interested in the one Canadian route. Rightly or wrongly I gained the impression that the company was so interested in the United States route that it was not at all concerned about finding the best or cheapest Canadian route. It was quite evident that the company's interests lay in an all-American route.
A promise was given that a route through the Yellowhead pass would be considered. We were told that the company would require to spend at least two months in studying it before they could give us an approximate idea of what the cost of such a route would be. We were informed that the company had spent well over a quarter of a million dollars in surveying the routes outlined and that it had been three years in doing so. There was no evidence that they were likely to spend the time necessary to make a thorough study of any other Canadian route than the one presented to the committee. If this particular company is to get its charter from the house and secure permission to build a line in the very near future, they will not be able to give due consideration to other Canadian routes. I see very little prospect of this company studying or surveying alternate Canadian routes unless their charter is delayed for a year or two in order to give them time to do so.
This company appears to be a very capable, well-managed subsidiary of a United States company. Some seventy-five or eighty per cent of the capital necessary for this pipe line, we were told, is to be raised in the United

States. Some seventy-five or eighty per cent of the gas transported by the line will go to the United States. In the light of those facts, and in the light of the quite evident interest of this company in the United States route, I see very little prospect of getting this company to build an all-Canadian line.
The question, of course, is whether the board of transport commissioners will order the company to follow an all-Canadian route. It was made quite clear to us that they would do so only if ordered by the board. In that connection I think we are placing upon the board of transport commissioners a responsibility that rightly belongs to this parliament. As western members have pointed out, the building of a pipe line is a matter of great concern to western Canada. I do not believe this government should leave the choice of that route to any private company. This matter is of such importance to Canada that I believe the government, through its engineers and geologists, should have some part in finding the most economical route for the line through Canada. A private company is interested in exporting as much gas as possible by the shortest feasible route, with the aim of making the greatest possible profit, and I do not think we have a right to expect such a private company to spend money in order to find out which of these routes will be most beneficial to Canada as a whole. That is not their job. Their job is to make money for their shareholders. I believe it is the responsibility of this government, as custodian of our natural resources for the benefit of our people, to take some steps to see that if our natural resources are exported, that export is done in the way that will be most profitable to this country.
We were told that a Canadian pipe line might cost $17 million more than a line through the United States. Well, $17 million may not be an exorbitant price for Canadians to pay in order to have that natural resource delivered through their own country, to promote the development of this country in the years to come. It has been pointed out already that if the fathers of confederation had taken the view now held by this company when it came to building the railway that was to connect Canada east and west, unquestionably they would have gone through the United States. But they did not take the view that the easiest and cheapest route must be followed. They were concerned with the future development of this country; and though the cost was greater, the railroad was built through Canada. It seems to me that this pipe line can be of enormous value to this country's future, and that the cost should

not be the major consideration but rather the interests of Canada as a whole, even though that cost may be $17 million greater.
I am not satisfied that this company has lifted a finger to find the most economical route through Canada. Personally I do not think they are interested in finding such a route. I think their main interest is in finding the shortest and cheapest route by which Canadian gas may be exported to the United States market. As the previous speaker said, I am surprised that the Canadian National Railways, in particular, seem to have taken no interest in this project. Goodness knows we have loaded the Canadian National with enough bankrupt enterprises, and overloaded it with the capital charges of bankrupt enterprises, so it is about time we gave the Canadian National some enterprise that had a prospect of being successful and making a profit. I think it would be in the interests of Canada that the Canadian National as well a-s the privately owned Canadian Pacific Railway should enter into a project so important as this to the development of our country.
We are charged, of course, with supporting a monopoly. Before the committee Mr. Dixon quite frankly pointed out that there was no prospect now or in the immediate future of more than one company building a pipe line to the Pacific coast, and that the line would be a monopoly, no matter which company got the charter. The only place where there is any competition is in this house, to see which company gets the charter, in order that two of the three may have a chance to fleece the public by selling stocks and bonds. As far as the actual pipe line is concerned it will be a monopoly whether built by this company or another. My own feeling is that parliament made a mistake in passing the pipe line bill without insisting that any company applying for a charter should indicate the route it intended to follow. I think no company should be granted a charter to build a pipe line anywhere it chooses, in order to export our natural resources to a market in the United States to promote the development of cities and industries in the United States at Canadian expense. I think no company, under any circumstances, should be left to designate the route the pipe line should follow. I believe it is the responsibility of this government to see that whatever company builds the pipe line, it is built only after there has been an adequate survey of all the possible Canadian routes.
I am not nearly as hopeful as the Prime Minister. I wish I could have as much confidence as he appears to have in the board of transport commissioners. I think we are
Alberta Natural Gas Company passing on to them a responsibility that thisr parliament should accept. I fail to see how that board could, of itself, determine that any pipe line is being built along the route which will best serve Canada, without some preliminary independent surveys and investigations having been made by government engineers. I greatly fear that the decisions in relation to these pipe lines will follow exactly the decision that was given regarding the oil pipe line which brought oil from Alberta to the east. There are a great many people in Canada, and in western Canada in particular, who believe that this government made a mistake in granting a permit to a United States company to build an oil pipe line terminating in United States territory instead of Canadian. I am afraid I have no more confidence that the board of transport commissioners will determine that these lines should follow a Canadian route any more than they did in the case of the oil pipe line.
One rather interesting feature in connection with this pipe line was brought out in the committee. It was pointed out to us by Mr. Dixon that this gas pipe line could be converted into an oil pipe line without very much difficulty, and in a comparatively short time. It was for this reason the company was asking for the privilege of building either a gas or an oil pipe line. Mr. Dixon pointed out to us that there was not much likelihood of this pipe line being converted into an oil pipe line except in case of war. In case of war, he said there would be a possibility that the conversion would be made. I think that is worth some thought on the part of Canadians. In the event of war in the foreseeable future, do we want a pipe line which conveys the major part of our gas through western Canada converted into an oil pipe line carrying oil down through the United States? I believe it is worthy of thought if one is looking into the future. History has a way of changing circumstances.
I would rather see this country have control of its own pipe line when it came to delivering oil in time of war. I believe that is one feature of this enterprise that should be taken into consideration, along with the other views that have been expressed. I suggest that this bill should be held up, and that the basic Pipe Lines Act should be-amended by the government. The government can bring in an amendment to that bill and' get it through this house oh short notice. A private member could not get that amendment through this session. The government could amend the Pipe Lines Act almost overnight, insisting that no company would get a charter until the line it proposes to follow

Alberta Natural Gas Company is indicated in the bill. Any company which has received the charter could be required to follow that course, and inform this house as to the line it proposes to follow. I believe this parliament has to take hold of this matter. It is slipping away from us, and it is slipping away from Canada. The fact that we let one bill through last year is being used as an excuse to let two or three other bills through granting charters to build pipe lines anywhere a company desires. I believe this government, and this parliament, has more responsibility to the Canadian people than to turn the distribution of these natural resources over to private companies, to do with them as they please, and for the most profit they can accumulate.

At this time, Mr. Chairman, I should like to explain to this committee of the whole house the reasons why I, as a member of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, came to the conclusions in committee that I did come to. Incidentally, the majority of the committee came to the same conclusions that I reached. Whether or not they followed the same line of reasoning as I did, I am unable to say.
As I understand it, we of the committee were there to hear the evidence adduced; to weigh and consider that evidence; and, on the strength of that evidence and of the arguments presented in the committee discussions, to arrive at a conclusion. I might say that I felt that no small part of the job was to sift out the irrelevancies and to decide what was and what was not applicable to the matter in hand. We, of course, had to try to come to a conclusion-at least, I felt that I did- on the basis of what was in the interests of Canada. The interests of these applicants or of any of their competitiors are of no concern of mine. But the interests not only of the district of Skeena, of the province of British Columbia, and of the province of Alberta but those of Canada as a whole were, and rightly should have been, the interest of all of us concerned.
In this particular case, of course, the interests of British Columbia and Alberta are particularly closely affected, but they are ndt solely affected. When we come to base an opinion upon a proposal, I suppose that all of us do so largely whether we feel that the person telling the story or outlining the proposals is sound, competent and reliable. In other words, is the witness credible? Ought we to believe him? What I want to do this evening is to try to outline the evidence which was presented to the committee and upon which the majority of the committee came to its conclusion.
Alberta Natural Gas Company
At the start of the hearing on this bill, there was presented to the committee and distributed amongst the members of it a memorandum signed on behalf of the applicant company. That was read to the committee by Mr. Connolly, who is one of the incorporators, one of these persons mentioned in section I of the bill; and he acted as parliamentary counsel for the applicants in this connection. In this memorandum there are several sentences which I think should be drawn to the attention of the committee. In the section which outlines the whole project generally, after dealing with supplying the consumers of Alberta, the memorandum goes on as follows:
... to transport such surplus gas as may then remain available to the Pacific coast to serve first the maximum number of consumers in British Columbia who can be reached economically, and, secondly, with such gas as remains available to serve consumers in the United States Pacific northwest. It is necessary to include United States market because the limited market available in Canada would not in itself support the cost of a pipe line from any of the known Canadian natural gas fields to Vancouver.
Those two statements are absolutely clear and unequivocal. We in the committee had to come to a conclusion as to whether or not those incorporators mentioned in section 1 of the bill are not fit persons to become incorporated as a body corporate in Canada. Are they financially responsible and sound businessmen or are they a fly-by-night concern purely for promotion? The statement and Mr. Connolly's evidence showed that they were adequately and soundly financed; that Morgan, Stanley and Company had undertaken to underwrite the full construction costs of the project concerned, and that four outstanding Canadian investment banking concerns were associated with them in that, and Mr. Connolly had letters from all of those associations of those businessmen backing up that statement.
Then there was the question as to where the actual pipe is to be made. Are we going to build a line with pipe manufactured in Canada or with pipe imported? The statement shows, and Mr. Connolly's evidence confirms, that arrangements had been completed with the Dominion Bridge Company for the supply of the large diameter pipe and with Page-Hersey Tube of Welland, Ontario, for the small diameter pipe, both of which would be produced in Canada from plate produced in Canada.
Only for the line in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have sat here with the most marvellous simulation of patience and listened to the flights of fancy of my hon. friends for a long time. I would suggest that they accord the same courtesy

Alberta Natural Gas Company to my statement of facts and reasoned argument. I want to say a word in connection with that pipe because I believe the hon. member for Greenwood quite unintentionally left an unfair impression this afternoon when he said that arrangements had been made for the supply of 400 miles of pipe; but he pointed out, and quite correctly, that that 400 miles of pipe would be required, irrespective of whether an all-Canadian or an all-American route was used. The evidence of Mr. Connolly and the memorandum showed that these incorporators have already expended the sum of $350,000 in geological, transportation and market surveys, which, to me at least, looks like some indication of a sound concern which meant business. Now we come to the question of routes, which does not really belong to this bill at all, because as has been so clearly stated, the general over-all Pipe Lines Act has definitely left, and deliberately left, the question of route to the board of transport commissioners. However, I think I am justified in mentioning the question of routes here for two reasons. First, it is, or is supposed to be, one of the main reasons for the opposition to this and , a similar bill; and secondly, it has certainly occupied a great deal of the time of the committee. On the question of routes Mr. Connolly said that his company, after some two years of preliminary survey and work, had data on five possible routes, one of which was an all-Canadian route. That is, an allCanadian route as far as Vancouver. From there it must go down into the United States. Three of them were alternatives of the first route, whereby the line would dip back and forth across the international boundary and take advantage of topography, and one can fairly be described as an all-American route. In that connection the memorandum says as follows-and this is certainly a matter of importance to anyone trying to arrive at a decision on this bill:
Matters touching engineering, terrain, cost of construction and maintenance of the line, the possibility of maintaining a continuous supply to consumers, markets, the price of gas to industrial, commercial and household users, are all matters which the board of transport commissioners must consider before any order is made approving a route.
