Now listen to this from the same memorandum:
The applicants for incorporation are prepared, if authorized by the board of transport commissioners, to build the first described route, which runs through Canada in its entirety to Vancouver. They are also prepared to build along any route which, after full consideration of all the facts, may be deemed to be in the best interests of Canada as declared by the board.
So far I have not mentioned the Yellowknife route-
Yellowhead.

The company stated quite frankly that they had given some consideration to the Yellowhead route-my mistake-and had not any detailed information on it. They said, through the president of the proposed company, that it would cost approximately $25,000 to make a detailed survey of the Yellowhead route, and they undertook to make such a survey before they appeared before the board of transport commissioners. So what do we get from Mr. Connolly's evidence? Mr. Connolly, as I have mentioned, is not only a parliamentary counsel, but one of the provisional directors of the company. He satisfied me, and I think he satisfied the majority of the committee, that he was sound and honest in his answers, and that he was definitely, and so were his associates, interested in prosecuting this proposition to a successful conclusion to the best interests of Canada as a whole. He satisfied me, and I think the majority of the committee, that the United States market is essential to this proposition; that if we do not sell to the United States we cannot sell on the coast because there is not enough market in British Columbia to justify the building of a pipe line.
He satisfied me, and I think the majority of the committee, that this concern was financially responsible, able and competent to carry out the work which they would undertake if they were given the power to do it. He satisfied me, and I think the majority of the committee, that the pipe which they would use would be made in Canada, in Canadian factories from Canadian materials. Ue must have satisfied practically everyone in the committee of the thoroughness with which the concern had investigated scientifically all the angles involved in this concern before they applied for a charter. He satisfied us that his concern would go before the board of transport commissioners with five, since extended to six, alternative routes, and that they would build upon such of those routes as the transportation board approved. He satisfied us that arrangements had been completed for the satisfactory collection of the gas in Alberta, and for the distribution

of that part of it which must be sold in the United States on the United States side of the line, and that companies had been organized to carry out both of these necessary details.
Now we come to Mr. Dixon. I suppose if there was one thing on which every member of the committee was agreed, it was that Mr. Dixon knew what he was talking about; that he was competent and capable. I have not the time to give this committee the full life history of Mr. Dixon, but I propose to give to this committee a short summary of it, and lest there may be any suggestion at a later stage, may I say now, that this summary of Mr. Dixon's career, together with all the rest of my speech, was prepared neither in Wall street, nor in Calgary, but is the result solely of my own efforts. This is Mr. Dixon: graduate of Harvard school of applied science, member of the firm of Brakow, Dixon and McKee, a firm in existence since 1919 as engineers in petroleum and natural gas and geologists. He has been a geologist since 1911. He has a very wide experience in construction and operation of pipe lines. He was geologist and engineer for the Houston gulf line from Corpus Christi, Texas, to Houston, the first such pipe line in the United States built by public financing. He started in 1924 his first work done for the American government during the first war. He has worked on many small enterprises, one of which grew into the United Gas Company, one of the largest in the United States. He was engineer and inspector on the pipe line from Houston to northern Louisiana in 1929.
There he was geologist for Southern Natural Gas Company, a pipe line about 800 miles long. For several years he was with the Missouri-Kansas pipe line which finally had some 3,000 miles of pipe line, counting double lines. He was one of the promoters of the Tennessee line from near Mexico to Buffalo. He was engineer for the El Paso line from Lea county, Mexico, to El Paso, and is still their consultant. He has personally investigated Alberta. He has been over the Kicking Horse, around the Big Bend, through Kamloops and down the Fraser; also from Radium Hot Springs to Cranbrook and Trail. He put in two summers of work in various possibilities between Alberta and Vancouver and hired other firms also to carry out some of this work.
Mr. Dixon's history and his personality and his bearing before the committee demonstrated most clearly that he was no fly-bynight promoter but a sound geologist and engineer who meant business. Now, as to routes. It must be remembered that Mr. Alberta Natural Gas Company Dixon is the president of the proposed company. He appeared before the committee and outlined the five routes to which I have referred. He told the committee the Kicking Horse pass route was utterly impossible at both ends. He admitted quite frankly that he had nothing but a superficial knowledge of the Yellowhead route. He undertook to have a survey made of that route to cost some $25,000, before any application was made to the board of transport commissioners.
He had detailed information of the Canadian route across southern British Columbia through the Crowsnest pass, and on the three alternatives thereof which, as I said, dip back and forth across the line to take advantage of good topography and avoid bad topography. In that connection here is an example of the evidence given by Mr. Dixon:
They have a route that has been constructed there through Allison pass and they estimated the cost of $4 million but it cost $12 million because, as they cut into the side hills, the hill moved across. That makes for very difficult pipe line construction. That is what makes the line more costly in going through the Canadian routes. It is just the difference in terrain.
I suggest that no one wants to be utterly obstinate in this connection. If it were considered advisable to route the line partially through the United States to get away from a condition of that sort, I wonder who would raise an objection, even on principle. It was just such detailed knowledge as that that impressed upon us the fact that Dixon had a sound scientific and practical knowledge, not only of the business as a whole but of this proposition in particular.
Mr. Dixon had fairly complete figures on the cost of construction, as complete as they could be when subject to approval as to any particular route. Mr. Dixon gave us some figures which were interesting and others which were far from pleasant. It might be interesting to note that their estimate of the cost of the all-Canadian route through the Crowsnest pass, including compressors and everything, was $92 million to be spent in Canada and $18,500,000 to be spent in the United States, or a total of over $110 million. But the figures which will be of more concern were the comparative figures of the actual cost of construction of a line from the Alberta gathering point to the Pacific coast. The figures for the all-Canadian and allAmerican routes were $78 million odd and $61 million odd, respectively. Whether those figures are pleasant or not, they are unfortunately authentic and we have to take them into consideration when we consider this particular proposition.
Mr. Dixon brought out evidence as to the additional cost which it might be expected

Alberta Natural Gas Company would have to be borne by consumers in the Vancouver district should it be necessary to build the more expensive line. He stated quite frankly that it was impossible to estimate exactly but that the figure would be somewhere between $700,000 and $1,200,000 which the consumers in the Vancouver area would have to pay year by year as a result of the more expensive construction. He was brought back later to this same question by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, but Mr. Dixon refused to change his estimate. As I said, Mr. Dixon did not have at that time up-to-date and detailed data on the Yellowhead route. However, on the second day of. his evidence when he was pressed for full details about routes he gave the following answer to this question which was asked:
Notwithstanding the fact that the Alberta Natural Gas Company have made a preliminary survey of five routes to the Pacific coast, if the board of transport commissioners determines that one or more routes covering different areas would be to the best advantage of the Canadian people having arrived at the decision that the gas will be economically saleable on the west coast, would they be prepared to build a pipe line on some such route as the board of transport commissioners may determine?

We would.
That is both clear and unequivocal, and so is this question:
With regard to the Yellowhead route, which has been mentioned on several occasions as being one possible route, would Mr. Dixon say that his company would be prepared to build a pipe line on the Yellowhead route if the board of transport commissioners instructed him to do so?

I have already answered that and
my answer is yes.
A little later another member directed Mr. Dixon's attention to the paragraphs in the memorandum dealing with routes and Mr. Dixon expressed his opinion in these words:
We would be willing to build on any route the board of transport commissioners would direct.
In case any hon. member may wish to raise the question that they cannot go to the board of transport commissioners and say, "You tell us which route we are to build on", I would remind the committee that they can make five or six applications. Those applications can be filed all at once-other companies have done the same thing-and they could build on the one approved. The question of routes is not quite as simple as it might appear. It does not do very much good for any of us to get up and wave our hands and say, "That route should be followed in such and such an area". We found from Mr. Dixon's evidence, and he knew, that there is a lot more involved in a route than just the building of the pipe line. There is the matter of maintenance to be considered, a matter of prime importance because gas must flow continuously through the pipe line from the time it starts to operate.

In general terms, there is no equivalent in the gas business to the emergency or reserve storage facilities available in the oil business. If a gas pipe line breaks, the service is disrupted. Not only is there no gas at the point of consumption until such time as the pipe line is repaired; it is necessary to take considerable precautions against a possible catastrophe by making certain it is safe to turn the gas on again. There is not only the cost of construction; that also is one of the reasons why the terrain through which the line must go is a matter of such real importance.

Will the hon. member permit a question? Are you stating that Mr. Dixon said that if there is a break away back in the line it immediately cuts off the gas to the consumer? He did not say that. The answer is that the gas piped at 1,000 pounds pressure would continue to maintain the supply for a long time and give him, time to repair the break.

I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member who has taken this, perhaps his first opportunity, to address the committee on this subject might give his ideas, which perhaps may be better than Mr. Dixon's, when I have finished giving mine.
I asked you if you were quoting Mr. Dixon to that effect.

If it is necessary for the hon. member for Calgary West to get information from me to complete his knowledge on this subject would he mind if I requested him to ask me when I have finished with the line of argument which I am pursuing at the moment, whether it suits him or not. There is another factor of this subject which up to the present has not been discussed very much. It was brought up by questions in the committee by the hon. member for New Westminster. I refer to the fact that there is a real possibility of United States gas supplying the market at Seattle and Portland. There is a very real threat that wells may come in in Wyoming which will make it practical for the United States to supply its own market. In that case it would be impossible for anybody to finance a line from Alberta to the Pacific coast of British Columbia. In that case the Americans might or might not supply the city of Vancouver and other British Columbia markets, but whether they did or did not the province of Alberta would have lost its market for the gas which at the present time it has for sale.
Hear, hear.

There is another unfortunate feature of this subject but one which we must consider if we are going to

try to consider the matter rationally at all. If it were possible it would be a very nice thing to say: We will put a pipe line through some undeveloped or partially developed country and because that pipe line is there we will develop a country which is not developed. Unfortunately that is not possible. You have to have your market there before you can build a pipe line to serve it. On that question I should like to refer to what Mr. Dixon had to say. I have no apology to offer for quoting him because it is Mr. Dixon's company we are considering. Mr. Dixon said at page 87 of the proceedings of the committee of April 27:
You cannot build a line relying on what might happen. You have to have your market there before you can build a line, otherwise no one will finance it. The returns are small and you cannot take the risk and have the line there eating its head off in interest and in depreciation without a market.
Either that is true or it is not. Whether we like it or whether we do not makes no difference as to whether or not it is true. Personally, with my small knowledge of Mr. Dixon's reputation, and from the apparent common sense of his remarks, I am inclined to believe that it is true. Later on with reference to Trail Mr. Dixon had this to say:
This projected line will go through Trail, where there is already a wonderful market for gas. The figures given to us by officials from the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company are to the effect that there will be 3 billion a year as a minimum and 5-3 billion a year that they say is possible depending, as I said yesterday, on some developments that are going on there now, whether they can use the gas satisfactorily.
Mr. Dixon's evidence showed that their proposal was to serve what might be generally termed as the Vancouver, New Westminster area. Here may I say, to avoid later misunderstanding, that he made it clear that they did not intend to build a pipe line into the Fraser valley, but that the British Columbia Electric Company desired to build a pipe line into the valley and to take the gas from the Alberta Natural Gas Company. I do not know why that should be a cause for levity. That was Mr. Dixon's evidence before the committee. They would serve the Vancouver, New Westminster area together with approximately 32,000 people in the Nelson, Trail, Rossland, Kimberley, Cranbrook area.
As to the proportion of the gas to be sold in British Columbia and to be sold in the United States, apparently that does not depend at the .moment on the amount of gas available, which is almost unlimited. It depends upon what the market is. Figures on the Canadian market were presented to
Alberta Natural Gas Company this company by the British Columbia Electric Railway Company which I understand will do the retailing, and by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. They are as follows: The Canadian market can absorb 11 h billion cubic feet per year plus 2-3 billion if Consolidated use their larger estimate. The United States market can absorb 63J billion cubic feet per year. It should therefore be obvious that if Alberta gas is going to be sold on the Pacific coast arrangements must be made so that it can be sold in the United States as well as in Canada.
Then there was Mr. Dixon's evidence in connection with the pipe. He supported Mr. Connolly that arrangements had been completed with both the Dominion Bridge Company and the Page-Hersey Tube Company, Canadian concerns, for the purchase of pipe in Canada, and that they had correspondence -in fact he produced it-confirming that that was possible and would and could be done. On all phases of his evidence Mr. Dixon stood up to what I think it is fair to say was a very severe cross-examination by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and others. It was impossible to shake him in his knowledge, because it was knowledge, of the facts. He impressed me on the occasions where he had not any personal knowledge and refused to hazard a guess but quite frankly stated that that was a subject beyond his immediate knowledge and therefore he was unable to give a firm answer. That is the sort of thing that creates a much better impression with me than if he had held himself out as one of those people who know the answers to every question under the sun.
There is an aspect of this matter which has been bothering many Canadians, and I think quite legitimately. It is a matter that I believe should be taken into consideration. They have been worried, and perhaps with some cause, whether enough consideration was being given to the future requirements of Canada, not only the market today but what it may be ten, twelve, or some other number of years in the future. That question was put to Mr. Dixon and he had this to say at page 121 of the proceedings of the committee on April 27:
Future needs. We have discussed and will discuss with the vital companies and authorities to try to get as nearly as possible what the consumption oi gas say for the next fifteen or twenty years will be, and that amount of space will be reserved for Canada.
There is another most legitimate cause of worry to Canadians and that is the idea that possibly somehow or other it might happen that United States consumers might get their gas and Canadians might be left without gas. It has nothing to do with the order in which

Alberta Natural Gas Company various places on the line are served. There is the fear that if the line is in the United States and these outlets are in the United States it may be possible that we may sell our gas to the United States and And that we have not got enough for ourselves. That matter was brought up and at page 122 Mr. Dixon was asked this question:
Is it a correct interpretation of that statement to say that it would give priority to the Canadian markets over the markets in the United States?
A. I would like to answer your question this way: there will be a priority on the Canadian market for their potential needs, and the rest of the pipe line capacity will be reserved for the American needs.
Q. It does not follow from this statement that you intend to serve markets in the order given in the statement, Alberta first, British Columbia second and the United States third?
A. When you have a pipe line and there is enough gas in the pipe line, it is not a question of who gets it first. Everybody gets it. But when gas is scarce due to some calamity or break or something of that order, nearly always there is a cut-off of the industries for the moment. I think no one would object to that. There is a cut-off so that the domestic consumers can be kept going. But as far as we expect, the Canadian market, up to a certain limit which would be as large as was needed, will have the priority. We have to have it in that way because otherwise we would never get by the federal power commission. There would be two markets, one called the Canadian market and one called the American market.
So what did we of the committee get from Mr. Dixon's evidence? First, I think he established to the satisfaction of all that he is a practical geologist with experience in and knowledge of all phases of the industry. I believe he established that so completely that should any hon. member attempt to belittle the standing of Mr. Dixon now he would find that he was actually belittling himself. He established to our satisfaction that he had detailed information on five alternative routes, one of which was all-Canadian, three of which were predominantly Canadian, and one of which was all-American, and that he had no authentic information on the Yellow-head route. He undertook to our satisfaction to get that authentic information on the Yel-lowhead route before proceeding with the application. He demonstrated to us a full knowledge of the costs of construction, and explained to us what I for one did not realize before, the important bearing of maintenance costs on the final cost of the gas. He undertook-and it was an undertaking-that all six routes would be submitted to the board of transport commissioners, and that the route approved by the board would be followed if his company were given the right to build it. He impressed upon us the importance of terrain in connection with maintenance cost and in connection with maintaining a steady flow.

Then he did not volunteer this, but as a result of his answers he impressed upon us the imminent danger of United States competition. In other words we might wake up some morning and find that Portland and Seattle are to be supplied by United States gas producers, while we have been sitting here talking about it. He established that an existing market was a prerequisite to the construction of a line. He satisfied us that his company was prepared and intended to serve the Vancouver and Kootenay areas with pipes made in Canada; that the future requirements of Canada were being allowed for and protected, and that at the moment the Canadian market has priority.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that as a result of the evidence given by these two witnesses before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, that committee was fully justified in reporting this bill, which is the same as saying that in its opinion these incorporators were a fit body of men to be formed into a company with power to apply to the board of transport commissioners for the right to build an international pipe line.
Now may I add just one or two thoughts of my own. I suggest to the committee that this matter is of a seriousness which perhaps some have not fully realized. We are dealing with a long-term proposal which embraces the whole future, as far as fuel is concerned, of a large section of British Columbia; and the whole future, as far as markets are concerned, of an important product of Alberta. This subject is too important to be debated here with vague generalities. Certainly it is too important to be discussed on the basis of ill-founded rumours or partial and distorted truths. I suggest with great respect to hon. members that we are in danger of not being able to see the forest for the trees, that we are overlooking the main object of this whole thing. The purpose of this legislation is not to build a pipe line. The building of a pipe line is not the be-all and end-all of what we are discussing today at all. We are discussing means of getting natural gas to the Pacific coast market, and the construction of a pipe line is merely incidental to that.
A pretty important incidental.

I grant you that it is an important incidental, since you cannot get it without a pipe line. But it might be delightful to build a pipe line anywhere. The point is that we must build a pipe line to attain this great objective of delivering gas to the Pacific coast market. Therefore we must not only consider the pipe line. We could build a beautiful pipe line anywhere and just walk away and leave it, and it would not be

worth anything. We have been so busy talking about a pipe line that many of us have forgotten that to some extent we should be interested in getting Alberta gas a market on the British Columbia coast; and I for one am impressed, and not pleasantly, by that threat of United States competition. I should hate to think we in this parliament had been in any way responsible

and I might be just as responsible as anyone else, since I am talking about the issue and not about personalities-for delaying this development so long that the Americans may decide to serve their own markets. The staunchest opponent of this bill-and there are honest opponents of it-I am sure will admit that we have to get into the United States market or we cannot build the pipe line at all.
The question of routes has come up, and I am going to make a statement that it would be much better policy for me not to make at all. That is, I am very much afraid that the Yellowhead route cannot serve the district around Trail. I wish to heaven that were not true, because the Yellowhead will come a good deal closer to my district than any route through the Crowsnest pass, but as yet no one has been able to satisfy me that they can reasonably connect the proposed Yellowhead route with the Trail district.
So for my part I am asking just this, that we allow these matters to be settled on the basis of their engineering, factual and cost data. I hope to heaven this line can and will be built in Canada, and I am very strongly of the opinion that it can and will be. But I for one am not willing to stand here and say that my pride as a Canadian will not permit them to take a dip of twenty or forty or sixty miles in the United States should it be necessary to get around Anarchist mountain or some other topographical hold-up which would add millions of dollars to the cost of construction.
Now I want to say just a word in connection with the claim that has been made that refusing to pass these bills would result in the creation of monopoly as far as Westcoast Transmission Company is concerned. That is the situation. If these bills are not passed the law as it stands today gives Westcoast Transmission Company the power-I do not say they are going to do so-to build just what the opponents of this bill do not want; that is, a line through United States territory. There has been a lot of talk and a great deal of criticism of the Westcoast Transmission Company. No one will believe me, I suppose, if I say I believe in a little honesty in debate once in a while. I am willing to admit that some months ago I was of the opinion that the Westcoast Transmission Company were, to some extent, opposing this and similar
Alberta Natural Gas Company bills. To be frank, I thought that opposition might be based either on their inability to meet competition, or their fear that their plans might not, in the long run, really be in the best interests of Canada. I want to categorically absolve the Westcoast Transmission Company, or in so far as I am concerned, from any such accusation. It is not, and could not, be better stated than it was by that company's solicitor in the Senate committee on Wednesday, October 19, 1949. I would remind the house that up to that time the Westcoast Transmission Company had been opposed to this bill. On that occasion Mr. D. P. McDonald said as follows:
Hon. Senators, the petition in opposition to the bill presented by the Westcoast Transmission Limited was prepared and based upon the fact that the proponents of the Alberta Natural Gas Company intended to build their pipe line through the United States. In the evidence which they have adduced before the committee they have indicated that they have planned a pipe line entirely in Canada and are prepared, if it is in the interest of Canada, to proceed with the pipe line in Canada. In view of this statement, the basis for the petition by my clients, which was that the interests of Canada required a pipe line to be constructed wholly in Canada before entering the United States, is not now applicable. Under the circumstances, therefore, I am instructed, with leave of the committee, to withdraw the petition as presented.
I think it would be equally fair, Mr. Chairman, at this time to meet another unfair criticism which has been directed at this Alberta Natural Gas concern. I have not the quotation but I do not think anyone will doubt that it has been suggested that this company has restated its views on this question as a result of the debate which occurred in this house during the last session, and which has been taking place during part of this session, to the effect that they were "all-American" until such time as this debate indicated it was poor business to be "allAmerican". That statement is also untrue because before this or the preceding debate ever commenced, on October 19, 1949, Mr. Dixon said to the Senate committee:
One of the routes Is entirely in Canada; all of the routes have a common starting point, near Fincher Creek, at a point near Yahk, British Columbia. One route follows an almost straight line from Yahk to the town of Osoyoos, hence to Princeton, then south to the border of the United States, hence to Holden, hence to Apple Grove, hence to New Westminster and Vancouver. That is the Canadian route, and it has a branch to Spokane.
Then he went on to outline the other routes just as they are at this time. It is not fair, therefore, not honest or just, to suggest that these people have changed their tune to suit some supposed political wind. I hope it is equally unfair to suggest that the opponents of this bill are opposing it because it might be found, in the long run, that some of their

Alberta Natural Gas Company pet theories are also not wholly in the interests of Canada. In so far as the West-coast Transmission Company is concerned, I wish once more to state that I absolve them from any such idea.
It has been suggested, Mr. Chairman, that in so far as British Columbia is concerned it is becoming increasingly popular to consider turning down these bills. On more than one occasion that has been suggested to me. Presumably the inference which I should draw is that if I hope to have success in another election it would be a good plan to do that which is popular. I do not want to indulge in any heroics about this, but so far as I am concerned I am far more interested in what is right, what is good and economically sound in the long run for the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta, than I am in anything that might happen to be popular at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I do not live in British Columbia, but I have a number of friends and acquaintances whose judgment I respect. I find that the thing which concerns them now is not where the pipe line is to be built, but how soon they can get oil, and how cheaply they can get it. As one put it in a letter, he does not give a blank where the line is built, as long as he can get gas and oil as soon as possible at the lowest possible cost. I think the general public should know that the dominion government is not paying for this pipe line, but I believe the people who are paying for it should have some say as to where it should go. Of course I should say that this government is paying something for the pipe line, because it has to pay for this discussion and filibuster.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something about the way in which this bill, and the other pipe line bill, were dealt with in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. In the past five years I have been a member of quite a number of committees, but I have never seen one run in the way in which this committee was run. After we had partially, and only partially, heard the evidence of two witnesses for the one company, what amounted to a closure procedure was adopted. We were prevented from hearing the complete evidence these witnesses could have given, let alone calling any other witnesses.
The member for Coast-Capilano said a few days ago that he was surprised that Dr. Hume, the outstanding authority on natural gas reserves in Canada, had not been called. As I have said, we did not even have the opportunity of completing the questioning of Mr. Connolly and Mr. Dixon, to say nothing
[Mr. ApplewhaiteJ

of calling Dr. Hume or any other expert. During the comparatively long debate which has ensued on this pipe line measure, speaker after speaker on the government side of the house has said that we should give these bills second reading and let them go to the committee. There could then be a full discussion in the committee, and members could obtain all the details. Actually, that is exactly what we did not get. It seems to me that the committee system, as I have known it during the past five years, was made a complete mockery by the way in which those two particular bills were pushed through without any reasonable amount of evidence being heard.
I have always understood that democracy is government by free discussion. The action of this committee was the complete negation of that principle. We were not allowed free discussion. We were not allowed what most of us have looked upon as our democratic right as members of parliament, the right to question witnesses who come before a committee, and secure the information we wish to have. As has been indicated before, that action was taken largely at the instigation of the member for Winnipeg South Centre. It was one which I hope he is now ashamed of, and which I hope will never be repeated in any committee of this house. The fascist and communist idea is that government by means of discussion is too slow and too inefficient. They do not allow government of that kind. We have had a taste of that sort of thing in this committee.
I was very glad to hear the speech of the member for Coast-Capilano the other night. He summarized in a complete fashion the arguments which those of us who have been opposed to these two bills have been putting forward for many months. In view of that excellent summary he gave, I do not think it is necessary for me or for anyone else to summarize again the reasons for our opposition to these two bills, and the reasons why an all-Canadian route is incontestably in the best interests of Canada and is one which we should ensure is followed by exercising the powers which we have as a parliament of altering the charters as they are presented here, to make sure that an all-Canadian route is followed.
I should now like to say something about some of the arguments that have been advanced and some of the statements which have been made by a number of the speakers during the past week. The hon. member for Edmonton West made quite a good speech. As a matter of fact, in many respects it was quite the reverse of the speech that he made previously, and I was glad to see that. Like the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, the only

thing that I disagreed with was the ending. He said he was going to vote for these bills, although he made an excellent speech which would persuade most people to vote against them.
That should be corrected, should it not, Mr. Chairman?

As I copied it down at the time the hon. member for Edmonton West was making his speech he said, "We heard evidence from experts". I should like to know who those experts were. We heard the evidence of one expert-an expert-and that is all. In addition to that, we heard the evidence of another man, that of Mr. Gilman, who is an engineer. But he admitted that he had never built a pipe line. I therefore do not think that he can be classed as an expert.
The only expert we heard was Mr. Dixon. I think it is quite apparent that if you hear the evidence of one expert only you do not get a good picture. In connection with this evidence that Mr. Dixon gave, as I say, we did not have any other experts there to contest the figures he gave us or the other statements he made. Certainly the costs that he gave were unduly slanted so as to indicate that it would be considerably cheaper to build this pipe line down through the United States than to build it by an all-Canadian route, although he had never made any survey of a Canadian route except one which runs straight along the border and which goes through some extraordinarily difficult country, as anyone who has been down in that part of the world knows.
As a result, the figures given by Mr. Dixon were not, I think, ones that should be swallowed holus-bolus. Certainly they should not have been swallowed until the committee had heard evidence from some other experts either corroborating those figures and costs given by Mr. Dixon or refuting them, particularly in view of the fact that these figures and costs and so forth were quite evidently given with the idea of showing that the American route was the best route as far as that company was concerned; and it was the one they wanted to follow.
The hon. member for Kootenay East on May 1 stated that we should have confidence in our civil servants-by that, in this particular case, I think he meant the board of transport commissioners-that they will determine the best route and that we should leave it to them and trust in them to do that. That is an argument that has been given time after time here by many people. What it amounts to is that we should abdicate our responsibilities and our duties as members of parliament and turn them over to this
Alberta Natural Gas Company board of transport commissioners. In my opinion, if there is any responsibility and duty that members of the House of Commons have, it is in the matter of deciding on what you might call questions of policy which are going to have an important effect on the population of this country for fifty to one hundred years in the future, at least; and this is one of those matters. It is not a matter in which we should abdicate our duties and functions and turn them over to the board of transport commissioners. It is our job to decide here whether this route should or should not be an all-Canadian route, whether in the general interests of Canada we should insist that any pipe line should be built on Canadian soil or whether we are going to decide that we will let it go any place that the people who wish to build it want to send it, get it out of Canada as fast as possible, and at the minimum amount of good for the population of Canada.
On May 1 the hon. member for Vancouver South also stated, "We must get the first use out of our primary resources, including gas." I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if we grant charters to this company or the other one to let them go ahead and build the route where it is quite clear they want to build it, namely, down through the United States, the first use of our gas is just what we will not get. We will be at the end of the tap. At any rate, the people in Vancouver will be in that position; and in my opinion, the amount of gas they will get will depend, to a considerable extent, on how much gas is needed in the United States. Certainly, on the figures which were presented to us, if this route is built down through the United States, the best that could be expected is twenty-five per cent of the gas which goes through that line coming back into Canada and seventy-five per cent of it remaining down there for use in the United States, no matter what the development along the Canadian Pacific coast might be.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre on May 2 rose in his place and said that he took no part in getting this bill put through in the house or in the committee. If he did not take any part in it, I do not know what he was doing around the committee, all the time that we sat there, coming in and speaking to the members, giving them notes, and evidently instructing them and so on and so forth. In my opinion, he certainly was taking some part in trying to get the bill through; and he was extremely busy trying to accomplish that purpose during the time the committee was meeting.
This afternoon the hon. member for York-ton managed to use a great many words but,

Alberta Natural Gas Company as usual, without saying a great deal. He made a statement to the effect that all of us who were here in the last parliament were in favour of the general pipe lines bill under which this charter is asked. That statement is not correct. I was here at that time. I interrupted the hon. member and stated that I moved an amendment to that general pipe line bill for the purpose of protecting the interests of the present consumers of gas in Calgary and throughout southern Alberta; and in fact throughout all Alberta, but those people in particular. But the government refused to accept that amendment. After quite a bit of discussion, they maintained that it was out of order, and it was finally so ruled; and I was not allowed to re-introduce it in another form.
I think that is sufficient to indicate that certainly all of us were not in favour of this pipe lines bill; I mean, the general pipe lines bill in the form in which it went through. As a matter of fact, looking back on it now as we who have been opposing these bills had freely admitted on many occasions, we made a serious error when that bill was put through in that there was not a clause written into it laying down that the route to be followed by any pipe line company must be indicated in their application for a charter. That was a serious deficiency. There has never been any disposition on the part of any of us to deny that it is a deficiency. Shouting at us over here, the hon. member for York-ton says, "You agreed with the principle of this bill. You all agreed with the principle of it." Certainly, we agreed with the general principle that the pipe lines bill should be put through under which it would be possible to control pipe line companies. But that is a different thing altogether from agreeing that the particular bill which was put in front of us was a perfect bill. It was not a perfect bill. As I said, I tried to amend it. One of the most important things which could have been in it, this matter of routes, was left out. It was far from being a perfect bill. But certainly we were in agreement with the general principle that a bill to control the building of pipe lines should be passed; and the passing of a bill was particularly urgent at that time because the rapidly-expanding production of oil in Alberta at that time demanded the construction of an oil pipe line to the east. This bill had to be got through before this company could be authorized to build. It was under that urgent necessity, and because it was the end of the session-and as a matter of fact, the end of parliament was only a few days away-that the general pipe lines bill and charters for the five companies which got them at that time were all pushed through.
[Mr. Harkness.l

The hon. member for Yorkton also said: "It is no use talking about routes here in the House of Commons." He said: "We could never agree on a route." Nobody has said that we could agree on a route. We have never tried to agree on a route. Nobody opposing these two particular bills has ever tried to say that here we should lay down definitely what the route should be for these particular pipe line companies. What we have maintained, and still maintain, is that it should be an all-Canadian route. That is all we asked in the beginning. That is all we are asking now. All we are asking is that it be an all-Canadian route. All this quibbling about our not being able to decide on a route here, as to where the pipe line should go because we have not the information, is just so mueh nonsense. We have never maintained that that should be done. All we say is that it should be an all-Canadian route, and that would satisfy us.
I should now like to refer to the hon. member for Cariboo. I find it somewhat difficult to say anything about him. He seems to be going around like a top these days. Perhaps it would be more proper to say that he resembles a whirling dervish. He made a speech this afternoon which seemed to indicate that he is now the strongest proponent of an all-Canadian route in the House of Commons. In the past he has been making speeches pooh-poohing any ideas we had along that line.
That is absolutely false.

He has been one of the strongest opponents we have had in trying to put over the idea that it must be an allCanadian route. In addition to that, on every opportunity that he has had he voted against an all-Canadian route. Therefore, as I say, he seems to be going round and round in circles, and I cannot tell just where he is.
He can't tell either.

The hon. member for
Skeena, as usual, made a very good speech. However, I am sorry to say that much of his premises and information was inaccurate.
Correct.

He started out by saying that Mr. Connolly and Mr. Dixon must have satisfied everyone in the committee that the most careful consideration had been given by them to all matters affecting the construction of the pipe line, or words to that effect. Well, what Mr. Connolly and Mr. Dixon had to say apparently completely satisfied the hon. member for Skeena, without his ever hearing evidence from any other

expert witnesses. He just took what these people said holus bolus and said: "This is what these people say; it must be right". He kept reiterating that time after time. He kept saying: "Mr. Dixon said this, and it was manifestly right. He told us this, and it is an incontrovertible fact." I do not think there is any question that we could have got two or three other witnesses as eminent as Mr. Dixon, possibly some of them more eminent, who I think would probably have flatly contradicted the assertions made by Mr. Dixon. This is another fact which shows that the hearing of only one expert witness in this committee was a very poor procedure to follow.
If the hon. member for Skeena would care to get a summary of the proceedings which have gone on for many months past this year and last year before the Alberta natural gas conservation board he would find in that a terrific mass of evidence by men who are conceded to be the greatest experts on the natural gas and oil business on this continent and perhaps in the world. If he went over that evidence he would find that a good many of the statements made by Mr. Dixon, and opinions that he has, are not shared by these other experts. I am not trying to say anything against Mr. Dixon specifically. We all know that experts are inclined to differ very frequently; particularly is that so in a legal trial where the question of insanity is involved, and the opposing sides bring in psychiatrists who state whether the individual concerned is sane or not. They always seem to be diametrically opposed in their opinions. I do not think it would be as bad as that with the experts in this natural gas business, but nevertheless there is a wide divergence of opinion on some points, and in that committee we certainly should have heard evidence from experts other than Mr. Dixon. In fact we should have had the evidence of Dr. Hume, and we should have had the evidence of at least one other outstanding geologist. But no; we were not permitted even to continue questioning Mr. Dixon.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question Did I not ask that Dr. Hume be called as a witness, and Mr. Theodore Link, and Mr. Stanley Slipper and Mr. Staver of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, and also a representative of the atomic energy commission of Washington?

I would say yes to the hon. member's question, and I would ask him in return, who was it that objected to their being called?
Alberta Natural Gas Company

The hon. member for Calgary West did not want Mr. Slipper and the other gentlemen whose names I have mentioned called. I say they will be called before the board of transport commissioners, if I have any power to call them before a route is determined.

The hon. member for Calgary West did not oppose anybody being called. I think the hon. member for Cariboo himself will admit that the reason none of these people was called, and that nobody was called, is that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre proposed a motion of closure that no further witnesses be heard, and the hon. member for Cariboo voted for it. The motion will be found at page 70 of the proceedings and evidence of the committee. I will not bother reading it. A list of the names of the people who voted in favour of not calling any further witnesses appears there.
Read it.
