motion?	[DOT]

I will read the motion:
Mr. Maybank, of the committee, moved:
That the committee adjourn until 11 o'clock, tomorrow, Friday, 28th April; that the one hour between eleven o'clock a.m. and twelve o'clock noon be used for continued taking of evidence and thereafter the committee proceed to a clause by clause consideration of the said Bill No. 7.
Then they put the closure motion and the hon. member voted for it. As I say, he is going around like a top. He tries to give the impression that he wanted to call more witnesses, and then we find him on the record as voting against even continuing to hear the witnesses we heard, let alone calling any more.
To come back to the hon. member for Skeena. He was satisfied, and he said that everybody must have been satisfied, that the most careful consideration was given to all matters. I say that is far from the truth. I was not satisfied, and many other members were not satisfied. I was not satisfied first of all as to where this gas was to come from. Mr. Dixon kept talking about getting all the gas they needed from the southern part of the province. There are only two gas fields that amount to anything in the southern part

Alberta Natural Gas Company of the province that are not being used. There is one at Pincher Creek and another at Jumping Pound.
What is the definition of the southern part of the province?

I will come to that. The gas from the Jumping Pound field will be needed for Calgary itself during the next 30 years. I must say in fairness to Mr. Dixon that later on he said he considered the southern part of the province to be the area from Edmonton south.
From 50 miles north of Edmonton.

Nobody else in Alberta [DOT]considers it along that line and I doubt whether Mr. Dixon did until this question came up. The hon. member for Skeena said that there were inexhaustible supplies of gas out there. He seemed to think that the question of how much gas there was was all settled, that there was nothing else to do but to just run your pipe into the ground and the gas would flow. That happens to be far from the truth. The Alberta natural gas conservation board has not yet decided that there is sufficient gas to look after Alberta's requirements for the next fifty years and permit export. These companies are trying to persuade that board to decide that question in the affirmative, but as yet they have not. I do not think that anyone who was not interested in getting gas from these two southern fields to the United States as rapidly as possible would ever contend there was enough gas to warrant the construction of a pipe line.
Most of the gas will have to come from what we in Alberta regard as the northern part of the province, from the area around Edmonton and to the north. I have no doubt that that is where most of it will come from.
I mention this matter because the hon. member for Skeena does not seem to know what the situation is in Alberta. He heard the [DOT]evidence of Mr. Dixon and then considered that everything was fine. He comes into the committee of the whole and makes a great defence of Mr. Dixon. I think the hon. member is a student and I recommend that he put some study on this matter.
We heard evidence from Mr. Dixon with regard to costs, but I was far from satisfied that the cost figures he gave were correct. For one thing he stated that the cost of the gas-gathering system in Alberta, which is really an integral part of the whole set-up, would be $26 million, and he said that he based that figure on steel costing $185 per ton. When he appeared before the Alberta natural gas conservation board he gave the same figure of $26 million as the cost of the


gas-gathering system but said it was based on steel costing only $150 per ton. I tried to find out from him why the figures were the same when the cost of steel was so much greater in the one case than in the other, but never got a satisfactory answer. I think that is an indication of how accurate his costing was. I think a great many of the cost figures that he gave were no more than what the succeeding witness, Mr. Gilman, called educated guesses.
Neither the Alberta Natural Gas Company or the other company would say what route they wished to follow. The hon. member for Skeena said that it was not necessary that they should state what route they wished to follow, that they could make five separate applications. That is a different story from what we got in the committee. The Prime Minister stated on Friday night that any company which put in five applications to the transport board and asked for a ruling as to which one they should follow would be laughed out of the board. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary West in the committee, anyone making application to the transport board would have to state a definite route. It is just nonsense what Mr. Dixon and Mr. Gilman told us when they said they were going to apply for several routes and let the transport board decide. They refused to state what route they fancied. When we tried to pin them down as to what route they would rather follow, they would not admit any one particular route.
As the Prime Minister pointed out, they could not put in five applications to the transport board for five different routes. Naturally their application would stipulate the route that they fancy. They are going to have to declare themselves, but we could not get them to declare themselves. I submit that the witnesses were not entirely frank with the committee, as some people would have us believe they were.
According to Mr. Dixon, Vancouver will require only 8 million cubic feet of gas per day. The city of Calgary uses some 20 million cubic feet of gas per day. Vancouver, with a population two or three times that of Calgary with the towns to the south including Lethbridge, is to get less than half the amount of gas. That is just ridiculous. Figures like that indicate that this particular company either is going to give Vancouver and the surrounding area the absolute minimum amount of gas and use the rest for the United States cities, or their figures are not just right. I think everyone will agree that Vancouver with its large population is bound to use more than forty per cent of the amount

consumed by Calgary. That was another
point raised in Mr. Dixon's evidence which I was not able to swallow.
This debate has been going on for some considerable time, but I think it has served its purpose to a large extent because it has provoked a large amount of public interest in this question of whether these pipe lines are going to go through Canada. I am convinced that the people who want to build these pipe lines through the United States will by the force of public opinion never be permitted to do it. Therefore this so-called filibuster has served an extremely useful purpose in that it has kept this question before the Canadian people for about a year and has mustered so much public opinion behind it that our future supplies of gas will be conserved for the use of Canada first, with the surplus going to the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Kootenay East who made reference to the proceedings of the committee and apparently they were satisfied with whar occurred there. I was far from satisfied myself because I felt that for a committee of that nature to call just one witness, ihe president of the company, an interested party, was not dealing fairly with the members of the committee. We could not get at the facts. We could not possibly get the truth from an interested party. We needed corroborative evidence, and we did not get it. We were blocked from calling such evidence.
I look at it this way. While the bill before us deals with a pipe line for gas, I look upon it as dealing with the lives of people. I look upon it as dealing with the lives of the people of British Columbia, their future welfare and the future development of that province. In my mind it has resolved itself into a question of whether we are to develop the state of Washington to the south of us or our own province of British Columbia. On it depends not only the material prosperity of our province but the future welfare of our youth as well. I know full well, as does everyone in this committee, that if these industries are developed in the state of Washington and not in British Columbia our youth will follow these developments, cross the border and become United States citizens. The only way we can keep them in Canada and make them good citizens is to see that their future is protected by having this vast energy, now about to be released for the use of man, made available first for the use of the people of British Columbia now and in future generations.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Coast-Capilano express his thoughts regarding the proceedings in the standing committee.
Alberta Natural Gas Company I had the same reaction. I realized quickly that British Columbia was being sold down the river in the light of the evidence of so-called experts of both companies. I am not questioning their integrity but I do question some of the evidence we are asked to accept as to their work in surveying a route in British Columbia. I should like to quote from the evidence of one expert. At page 213 of the proceedings of the committee he was asked the following question:
Q. In connection with the Yellowhead route the only observation you made was when you went through by train?-A. That is right.
Q. Now, I just want you to answer this question. How fast was the train going when you were making those observations?-A. Oh, about 20 to 25 miles an hour.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the type of evidence submitted to show that this company had some interest in putting through an all-Canadian route. The expert travelled over the Yellowhead route at 25 miles an hour and made pencilled notes from a train window. I do not know whether it was at night. We did not ask that question. The result is that they are not prepared to go before the board of transport commissioners with a proposition to build a pipe line along that route. Naturally I question such things. It does not appeal to me as common sense.
I realize, having listened to the evidence given by these experts, that the people of British Columbia are being sold down the river. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano pointed out that we already have three railways making the crossing through the Cascades, Selkirks and Rockies between Alberta and British Columbia. I am not sure whether there are two or three completed highways. There are already routes in existence crossing the Rockies and the other ranges, and each of them is capable of accommodating a pipe line route at the side thereof from Alberta to British Columbia. Naturally there are one or two routes suggested. I appeal particularly to members from the eastern provinces to consider seriously how they are going to vote on this measure. Members from British Columbia know their own province far better than members from eastern Canada. We know the terrain, we know the difficulties we are up against, and we are satisfied that the proposal to follow an all-Canadian route is a sound and feasible plan. Because of their lack of knowledge we appeal to them to take our word for it. I am sorry that they cannot get expert evidence on the matter because the work of the committee is now completed. On this basis I am asking them to support our provincial government and the people of the province of British Columbia against the financial

Alberta Natural Gas Company interests who seek to build a pipe line for profit rather than for the assistance of our people.
I should like to commend the Vancouver Sun and the Vancouver Province for their assistance in trying to get the pipe line constructed through our province. I should like to commend particularly the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Fraser Valley for the attitude they have taken, and especially the Vancouver members for their support of an all-Canadian route. It is quite possible that Vancouver could get cheaper gas by some other route, but Vancouver, one of the most prosperous cities of Canada, has become so because of the fact that the interior of British Columbia has made it so. We supply it with goods that are shipped out of there by rail, boat and aeroplane. We have kept it going for some generations. They know that a prosperous interior means a prosperous Vancouver. Some of the members from that city realize that. The city council realize it and fully endorse what we are trying to do. The provincial government has endorsed our proposition on behalf of the coast cities. Today I have received the endorsation of the council of the associated boards of trade of the whole of British Columbia. I do not propose to read the resolution, but it is endorsed by every board of trade except those on Vancouver island who were not at the meeting. They ask that an all-Canadian route be designated.

Will the hon.
gentleman read the resolutions from the associated boards of trade of British Columbia?
Read them. That will take forty minutes.

The first resolution is submitted by the associated boards of trade of the Fraser valley and lower mainland to the council of the associated boards of trade of British Columbia and reads:
Whereas applications are before authorities for the approval of route for natural gas transmission line from Alberta to the British Columbia coast; therefore be it resolved that the associated boards of trade of the Fraser valley and lower mainland request the government of the province of British Columbia to give full consideration to the location of the said transmission line so that it may serve the greatest possible number of communities in the interior of British Columbia, thus stimulating the expansion of industry throughout the province.
The next is a resolution submitted by the associated boards of trade of the southern interior to the council of the associated boards of trade of British Columbia concerning the route of the line. It reads:
Whereas the route chosen by the Westcoast Transmission Company through the Peace river district

and south through Prince George and the Fraser valley to Vancouver would benefit more people in Canada, especially British Columbia; therefore be it resolved that the associated boards of trade of the Fraser valley and lower mainland appeal to the other boards of trade throughout the province of British Columbia to unite in getting the provincial government and our federal members to advocate the route of the gas pipe line through central British Columbia to Vancouver.
Then there is this footnote applying to the two resolutions:
Both of these resolutions, considered as one at the discretion of the chair, were unanimously endorsed by delegates from all portions of the province excepting Vancouver island which was not represented, and are respectfully submitted for your consideration.
I am fighting for an all-Canadian route, not necessarily that particular route, although that will suit me fine.
You are opposing the boards of trade of the Okanagan.
You talked this afternoon.
I read the resolutions.
Why did you not quote the resolutions?
I submit that this resolution of the boards of trade of the province of British Columbia expresses the opinion of responsible businessmen.
What is wrong with that?
He is going contrary to it.
He cannot understand English.

Again I say that, unlike some members, the route of the pipe line means a great deal to my riding and I intend to fight for it in spite of other ridings that are not so keen about it. During the discussion of this all-Canadian route I was alarmed to find that the so-called expert had no idea that the Okanagan valley existed and that roughly 120,000 people lived there. He had not thought about it, had not surveyed it, did not even know where it was. So I claim that anyone coming before this house talking about an all-Canadian route who does not know of the existence of that potential market has. not given the matter a great deal of thought. In other words I believe the all-Canadian route was an afterthought, when they found the strenuous objection to such a route not being included in their proposals. And, as I pointed out, you cannot survey a route of that kind, through mountainous country, bogs and so on, from a train or car or plane. It has to be done on foot to be done properly, and this has not been done in the case of a single route through the interior of British Columbia by either of the companies whose bills are being considered.

It is true that figures were given as to costs, but that was merely guesswork. In spite of the statement made by the engineer the shorter mileage involved in an allCanadian route would more than make up for the extra cost. Whether it is built in British Columbia or in the state of Washington, the terrain is just about the same. You still have to overcome the Rockies, the Cascades and the Selkirks. They are practically the same in Washington and British Columbia; and actually the highest pass traversing the mountains to the coast is not in British Columbia but in the state of Washington.
For the past year we have been told that all our questions would be answered in committee. Like many other hon. members I hoped this would be true; but when we reached that committee we found it was not the railroad committee but the railroading committee. Certainly they railroaded it through without proper witnesses being called. Personally I doubt whether a serious survey was ever made of an all-Canadian route, from the evidence submitted. I am sure no survey of the potential market has been carried out, because even Nelson was an afterthought, though Nelson would be convenient to the route whether it went through British Columbia or through the United States.
Apparently this committee of which I was a member had no power to specify any route, or to change the bill in any way. We did not even have power to recommend a route. The only power we had was to listen to the evidence. Why that was so I do not know. I think it was a sheer waste of time for two or three days. And I claim the board of transport commissioners does not have a great deal more power. It has the power to scrutinize carefully and in detail all applications for licences, but that is all. It cannot say, "You must build through the Crows-nest pass" or by any other route. They are not engineers; they do not have a staff of engineers who have on file the details of various routes across Canada. They rely entirely upon the application being made at the moment, and the map accompanying that application. They must take it for granted that the data on the map is accurate, and it is on that basis that approval is given. It is not a matter of whim of the board, saying, "We do not like that route. We prefer the more scenic highway around Big Bend, so you must build in that direction." That is not it at all.
Frankly I am in a quandary as to the body that does control this matter of route. I have a very interesting article here on the same subject in Oil in Canada, a Canadian weekly
Alberta Natural Gas Company which claims to be the most widely read authority on Canadian oil, published in Winnipeg. It says:
In the House of Commons last Thursday, Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce, is reported by the Canadian Press to have said that the government will not allow Alberta natural gas to be exported to the United States before it reaches potential consumers in neighbouring British Columbia.
Then, after conveying the idea that the minister can determine the route, it goes on:
The Pipe Lines Act passed last year gives the board of transport commissioners authority over routing of lines, while parliament has control over incorporation of companies.
Se we have two possible controls over the route. Then at the end the editorial states:
The Alberta government has full control over the export of natural gas by its own legislation. Surely it is in a far better position than any other government or any potential consumer to judge what is the best method of dealing with its own natural resources.
The promoters of natural gas pipe line companies are familiar with the economics of supply and demand and the effect of construction costs on operating results. So far as we can recall, there has never been any suggestion that the Alberta government can't deal properly with the technical problems involved in making a decision whether to grant permission for gas export once a charter has been granted to a company.
So we have the committee, which I thought had power but had none; we have the board of transport commissioners, which I thought had power but apparently has not. Then we have the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who thought he had power, but apparently he has none; and the Alberta government have come out definitely and claimed they do have the power. But I have another statement that confuses the issue still further. This is from the Vancouver Province, headed "Mayhew backs Canadian route". It is quite an article, in which the Minister of Fisheries favours an all-Canadian gas pipe line from Vancouver to Alberta, and thinks an allCanadian route will finally be selected. But he says it will be the people who buy the stock in whichever company builds the line who will determine the route. So now we have five groups claiming to have that power. According to the Minister of Fisheries it is the stockholders, but we also have the Alberta government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the board of transport commissioners and the standing committee of this house. All the time the logical body to have that power is the parliament of Canada. We are the supreme body, and that power should be re-invested in us if we have turned it over to anyone else.
In the circumstances all I can do is appeal to whoever has the power to see that an allCanadian pipe line is put through. Let me
2296	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company quote still another point of view. I have mentioned five people or groups presumed to have some power over this route, but the hon. member for Vancouver South believes that public opinion will have that power, though just why I do not know. The hon. member said he had a great deal of faith in the petroleum and oil conservation board of Alberta. He intended to vote for these bills, but said he was going to do his best to build up an opinion in British Columbia that would demand that before any gas was exported to the United States the line proceed to British Columbia and end in Vancouver, as far as Canada was concerned. But this is the time to do that, not after the charter is granted. These people will not care a tinker's cuss about British Columbia once they have their charter. They are out for profit; and we must agree at once that the most profitable route is through the United States. But we are building our country for our youth, not for profits, and I claim our proposition is the proper one.
I was rather amused at the retort of one of the parties making application before the committee. He had been making obviously vague statements as to the route, and upon being asked for details, and why he was guessing at the cost price in Vancouver and the cost of the route without a proper survey, he said, "Well, it is like a horse race and I am entering a Canadian horse in this pipe line race." It seems to me he had a lot of donkeys to compete against. I do regret the lack of independent expert testimony before the committee. I am not questioning the integrity of the witnesses who did appear, but I do question the opinions given, because they were expressed by men who want to build a pipe line. If the committee pressed hard on any point they would agree to anything. After getting the charter they would agree that they would start to survey the Yellowhead route. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that such an obliging company as that is attempting to get our support in order to be done with the committee. They realized we were just a nuisance, and had no power.
What evidence have we that the company intends to build a Canadian route? A defence has been made tonight of Mr. Dixon. I am not questioning Mr. Dixon's character, but I do suggest that a closer reading of the evidence submitted by Mr. Dixon will not indicate one iota of evidence that shows this company intends to build a Canadian route. As I pointed out, part of the survey was made by train, part by car, and part by odd trips to here and there. Most of the evidence was based on a superficial knowledge, and in view of that I question it.


On Friday the Prime Minister stated that our protection is in the fact that each applicant has to file with the board of transport commissioners a map of the proposed route. That is quite true, and that is what we are worried about. If any company is granted a charter by this house, it is free to submit any one route. There is no compulsion whatever. It goes to the board of transport commissioners as a business concern with a business proposition. I am satisfied from the evidence submitted by this company that it. will favour the route through the United States. I know when the company comes to sell its shares the subscribers will not be satisfied with the evidence we got. They will want more detailed information and they will get it. In the action of the United States banking company I mentioned, which is prepared to underwrite the whole concern, you have an indication that United States people are interested in the route and the ultimate profits that will be derived from the undertaking.
In parliament we are supposed to protect the subscribing public, and also the consumer. Apparently we cannot assist either one. We cannot protect the subscribing public because-we were limited in the committee as I pointed out, and we cannot protect the consumer because there is no rule that an applicant has to prove to us the price at which the commodity will be delivered at any given point. As I said before, we are wasting time because-we lack powers. I am sorry that the Canadian National Railways did not see fit to enter this field, and render the service on a national basis, just as the railway does. It is the logical thing for a railway company to do, and not to wait for United States capital to-come to our province.
Another statement with which I take issue is the statement made by Mr. Dixon that it. does not necessarily follow that commercial development follows a pipe line. I should like to point out to him that history in the United States has proven that the different towns along the route of a pipe line have immediately been a source of interest to industries, and vast empires have been built, particularly in Texas and southern California.
I should like to draw to the attention of the members a booklet which they found on their desks, entitled "Canada's Oil, Edmonton Centre". On the second last page-I am not going to read them-there are indicated the industries that are available if power and raw materials are available. In Edmonton they have the power, but they lack the raw materials. In British Columbia we have the raw materials, but we lack the power. The-evidence on these two pages will show hon..

members the industries I have in mind that could be established on a prosperous foundation in British Columbia.
We have another vast interior area, the Cariboo. I really believe the Cariboo area has great possibilities. If the pipe line traversed the centre of that part of the country, one would find that these vast plains and undeveloped mines would develop rapidly. I frankly believe that if the member for Cariboo would support us in our contention that the pipe line should go through that area, he would be doing a service to his own constituency. The tendency today throughout the world, owing to the unsettled nature of our economy, seems to be to decentralize industry. I think you will find that condition, even in England, where the area for decentralization is very limited. Efforts are being made to take industries into places like Holyhead and Bangor in Wales. I saw them myself last summer, scattered all over the country, in order to bring an element of safety in case of war. The same thing applies to Canada. Industry should be taken away from the big centres such as Vancouver, Seattle and Tacoma. They should be moved into the interior where the raw materials are. It would be safer from the national point of view; conditions for the workers would be healthier, and it would be a cheaper haul for the raw materials.
By routing this pipe line through British Columbia, we would not only be increasing the earning power of our province, but we would be getting more revenue for the provincial government through income, provincial and corporation taxes. We could increase the population of British Columbia and give the people economic security.
I am going to ask the eastern Canadian members, and particularly the members who have not given this bill a great deal of thought, to consider how they should vote. The Prime Minister has said that the vote is free, and I appeal to you to use your free vote to do something for a province that is appealing to you for assistance. The councils of every town in British Columbia, the provincial government and the Legion in every town have endorsed our stand. The press of the province is behind us. I ask you to heed this and do what your conscience tells you is right. We are fighting for the province of British Columbia. Last year the proposal to build a bridge over the Canso strait was brought before us. The members from British Columbia did not question the need- for the bridge or the cost of it. We felt that the people in that area knew far better than we did what their own needs were, and we were prepared to support the measure. We know
Alberta Natural Gas Company our needs, and we are appealing to you to treat us in the same manner as we treated you on the question of the Canso bridge.
I know the statement has been made that a monopoly is liable to be created if these two companies do not get the line. But again, I should like to quote to you from the Minister of Fisheries, referring to the three companies proposing to build a pipe line from Alberta to the west coast. The minister said:
"I'd give them all their bills. They're all alike to me, and if one fellow comes along and says he'll build an all-Canadian route, that's the fellow I'd give it to."
The minister said: "If one fellow says he can build an all-Canadian route, there's no reason the others couldn't. They'd have to show us why they couldn't build it through B.C."
But the minister says:
Everyone knows there will be only one pipe line . . .
In British Columbia.
When you charge this particular company, which now holds the charter and is prepared to build through British Columbia, with having a monopoly that has no competition, I claim that from the statement of the minister-himself it would appear that it is not a question of monopoly, but of which company is going to get the monopoly. Personally, I do not care which company gets that monopoly. Apparently it is predetermined that it shall be a monopoly; but I am satisfied that whichever company gets the final charter to build through British Columbia, it will have the blessing of a million people in that province.

It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to take up many minutes tonight owing to the fact that, from listening to the debates on pipe lines over the last two years, one could almost believe that almost everything about pipe lines could have been said in that time.
I must congratulate the hon. member for Skeena who tonight covered the question of pipe lines, pipe line building, charters and so on from one end to the other. My purpose tonight in saying a few words is to make clear my intention with regard to how I will vote and why. It has been pointed out that one of these charters has been given to the Westcoast Transmission Company, and it seems only logical that these other two companies should be given these same opportunities. Because one company has been given a charter is no reason to believe that it will be the one which will receive the final say from the Alberta government. Believing in competition as I do, I therefore think these three companies should have the same opportunities. After this vote is taken, if the house then desires a Canadian pipe line, I
2298	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company believe they should turn their attention to the amendment which I have brought forward in Bill No. 132, which reads in part: ... a map showing the general location of the proposed line whereof the main line shall be located entirely within Canada.
If we pass these two applications which are before the committee, and then amend the Pipe Lines Act, which is the intention of my bill, I think it will take care of any further discussion.

This debate, Mr. Chairman, has in some ways been one of the most reassuring things that has happened in this country in quite a long time. Two private bills, or what were described as private bills, came before the last session of parliament. When they were presented as private bills it was suggested that it was a waste of time for anyone to point out that they should be dealt with in another way. When members tried to get some definite information as to exactly where these pipe lines were going and some assurance that our own Canadian interests would be served first, those who raised those points were told that they did not have much faith in their own committees or in the board of transport commissioners and that those were mechanisms that would protect the public in regard to these things.
From time to time members of the government have shown some irritation that this debate should continue, both during the last session and in the present session. The debate has been called a filibuster and, on certain occasions, the suggestions have even gone so far as to imply that those who were opposing these two private bills, in their present form, were serving some particular purpose and were seeking to establish a permanent monopoly in the hands of Westcoast Transmission Company which, by mistake- and it was by mistake-got a charter last spring at a time when this house was dealing all too hurriedly with certain public business, under assurances which were not fulfilled. That point I should like to recall, because it has a definite bearing on the discussion that is now taking place. At a time when everyone knew that we were in the closing hours of the last session, the overriding pipe lines bill was introduced, and along with it four bills to incorporate pipe line companies.
Five.

I will correct myself; several bills to incorporate pipe line companies were introduced. In the case of the Interprovincial, assurance was given that this was for the purpose of carrying oil to the refineries in eastern Canada, and that the reason that the pipe line in that case was going to
[Mr. Sinnott.l

Superior in Wisconsin rather than to the lakehead in Ontario was that of the economy and saving that would be effected.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We did not find it out until after the election.

What we did not find out until after the election was that the main purpose behind its going to Superior was so that oil could be exported to the Chicago area in the United States, and that while undoubtedly oil will be shipped to eastern Canada-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I wonder if the leader of the opposition would permit me to make clear the point of my interruption. My point is that we did not know at that time that the route was going to go outside Canada at all. All we were going to build then was simply a route from Edmonton to Regina and down to Winnipeg. It was only in the summer that we learned that it was to go down to Superior.
After the election.

The hon. member who has just spoken is correct. No detail was given until later as to the fact that it was going to Superior. But when that information was given, and when that was put before the board of transport commissioners as a reason for getting that route, the assurance was then given that this was an economy in shipping the oil to eastern Canada. At the present time we have two bills before us which we have been discussing all the way through as gas pipe line bills. Let us remember that these are oil pipe lines as well. The bills cover both oil and gas. As to whether gas or oil will be the main commodity carried in these common carriers only those who have the ultimate responsibility of operating the pipe lines can possibly tell. Both commodities are produced in the same area.
One of the reasons I said that this had been a very reassuring debate is this. Hon. members, who a comparatively short time ago were extremely critical of those who asked for any information and for assurances that Canadian interests were going to be served, have with great frankness and after very careful analysis of what took place before the committee stated that they are not now satisfied with the information that came before the committee, and that they are going to oppose these bills because of the way in which the information was withheld in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. That in itself is a demonstration that we have seen right here of democracy working, where the public have an opportunity to understand what is taking place, to express their opinion, and through that expression of

opinion to convey their own desires to the members who represent them in this house. There is much to be said for a procedure which gives the public time to understand exactly what we have before us for consideration here.
Hon. members will recall that when these bills were before us for second reading during the present session the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on more than one occasion, said that he could not understand the reluctance of hon. members to let these bills go before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where it would be possible to get all the essential information in regard to these proposed operations. Finally the bills did get second reading; they went before the committee, and hon. members who previously were supporting the bills have come into this house and have said that no real information came before the committee upon which they could say where these pipe lines were to go and whether the Canadian interests were being protected. By devices that have already been described in very unflattering terms by those very hon. members who previously supported these bills, the committee completed its work and the bills are now before the house.
On Friday the Prime Minister came back and we have a new appeal to the house. The committee has done its work. This is what the Prime Minister said to us. We should pass these bills so that they could go before the board of transport commissioners, where maps must be submitted and where details must be fully examined. That is the next stage. Hon. members were asked to give up their responsibility in the first instance to let this go before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and they know the results. Now that the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines has done its job and kept information from hon. members and from the public, hon. members are asked to pass these bills and leave it to the board of transport commissioners to do the job that we should do here. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is an affront to parliament. Either we have some judgment to exercise and some responsibility to assume or we have not. If we have no responsibility, these bills should not be before us. If we have no responsibility then, as has been previously stated, this should be dealt with by the Department of the Secretary of State and ordinary company charters should issue, and this should be dealt with without any pretence that members of parliament are passing judgment upon a matter so important as this.
But there is one point that has not been sufficiently discussed, and I do not believe 55946-146
Alberta Natural Gas Company it has been emphasized at all. The government has the final responsibility, and the government is answerable to parliament. There is an act of great importance which was passed in 1907, and it is still on the statute books. It is known as the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. Section 5 of the act reads as follows:
No person shall export any power or fluid without a licence, or any power or fluid in excess of the quantity permitted by his licence, or otherwise than as permitted by such licence.
2. No person shall, without a licence, construct or place in position any line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.
That is a positive prohibition. Section 6 reads:
Subject to any regulations of the governor in council In that behalf, the governor in council may grant licences, upon such conditions as he thinks proper, for the exportation of power or fluid where a right to export exists by lawful authority.
2. Such licence shall be revocable upon such notice to the licensee as the governor in council deems reasonable in each case.
Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the leader of the opposition, but it is now eleven o'clock. Unless he has unanimous consent he cannot continue.
If I may add one sentence to give meaning to that, it would not take me thirty seconds.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Has the leader of the opposition unanimous consent to continue?
Go ahead.

I think it would give meaning to these sections if I added this. These two sections mean simply this. Under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act of 1907, which is still in force, the government, which is the executive of this House of Commons, has the full responsibility for determining where a pipe line should be laid, whether it shall be laid, and under what conditions it shall be laid, if that pipe line in any way is to be used for the export of oil or gas. That brings the responsibility today, as it was then, right back to the government; and before any hon. member should vote on a pipe line bill the government should state its policy in definite, unqualified terms, and I believe that policy should be a clear statement of Canadian rights first, definitely assured, before any consideration is given to the exporting of these great resources upon which future development will so largely depend.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will move to go into supply with the hope of voting on the amendment of the leader of the opposition. If we are successful we will call three departments, post office, national health and welfare, and public works. For some time we will discuss the question of the denial of mail service to certain persons, which was brought up before. We would hope to take up certain small bills, the first being Bill No. 12, respecting grants of public lands, in the name of the Minister of Resources and Development. The second would be Bill No. 81, respecting crown lands

in Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. I might interject to point out to the leader of the opposition that this is not the bill he had in mind. He had in mind Bill No. 90, to amend the Northwest Territories Power Commission Act. I have looked at that act and find it has only two sections and perhaps we can take that one up as well. That would be three small bills in the name of the Minister of Resources and Development.
